subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to incorporate the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the purpose of (a) acting in the place of the Minister of Finance in the operation of the National Housing Act, 1944, and (b) providing discounting facilities for loan and mortgage companies; to provide for the appointment and salaries of the officers and staff of the corporation and the appointment and fees of the directors; to authorize the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of sums not exceeding twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000 J for the provision of paid-up capital for the corporation; to make available for the housing functions of the corporation moneys appropriated under the National Housing Act, 1944; and to make provisions with respect to the functions and powers of the corporation.
He said: His Honour the Deputy Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to.

maintopic: INCREASE IN APPROPRIATION FOR LOANS AND GUARANTEES

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1944, and to provide more particularly for an increase in the appropriation for loans and guarantees under Part II of the act for the payment out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund of loans and losses in respect of loans, not exceeding in the aggregate one hundred and fifty million dollars, and in respect of guarantees, up to an aggregate principal amount of one hundred and twenty-five million dollars of investments guaranteed.
He said: His Honour the Deputy Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to.

maintopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext:
I have a second question
to direct to the Minister of Labour. The long continuance of the labour dispute of the Ford Motor plant at Windsor and the failure to make any apparent progress in settlement, is, I am sure, causing concern to all members of the house and all interested in the future course of labour management relations in Canada. Would the minister indicate to the house whether any further steps to bring about a settlement have been taken? If not, would the government give consideration to having the Minister of Labour proceed to Windsor with a view to facilitating the settlement of this strike?

maintopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend knows
the situation at the moment. We are working very closely with the Ontario Department of Labour. An invitation went to both the employers and the employees to meet the provincial minister of labour and myself in the city of Toronto. But may I make this remark, which is equally applicable to the ministers of labour of all the provinces, that there is a physical limit to what a minister of labour can do and where he can be. That is why we built up our machinery, with a conciliation service which is as good, I think, as can be found anywhere else, to face up to a situation of this kind. I believe it is a fair observation, Mr. Speaker, if I may be permitted to make it, that both the Ford Motor company and the leaders of the employee's organization are grown-up men. The company have made the decision, rightly or wrongly-and I said, when I was last asked this question, rightly, in my opinion-that until the company's officers are enabled to get into the Ford plant they will not sit down with the trade union leaders. That attitude is related to a very old prin-siple: as I said the other day to one of the hon. members from Montreal, the Canadian's home is considered to be his castle. It seems to me that if some concession on the part of the trade union organization could be made

in respect to that principle, which has been enunciated by officials of the company-and after all, there are two sides to a medal-1 would be prepared, in fact I would have been prepared a week ago, to go to Toronto with my good friend the acting minister of labour of Ontario and endeavour to arrive at a settlement of this dispute.
.1 could speak at length on the fundamental principles involved in conciliation, and as to whether the company or the trades union want this or any other government to write a contract for them. I shall not go further into that matter at the moment, because I understand that it is an issue in the discussion, but when my estimates are up, or if it is raised by any hon. member, I shall be quite prepared to give an answer.
I say frankly and sincerely that the labour departments of both governments are anxious to bring this fight to a conclusion. We were very successful in such matters during the war. But may I say in a kindly way that this House of Commons is not the place to negotiate a trade union agreement, because of the political implications that are involved. I know that persons who hold certain points of view are anxious to see such action taken by democratic legislative bodies, but it is my belief that it would not only be physically impossible, but that it is not in the interests of democratic institutions and their proper functioning, as we understand these things.
I have to be very careful to-day, because, as no one knows better than my hon. friends opposite, in an industrial dispute what is said at a distance is sometimes misconstrued at the point where the dispute exists.
I reiterate that I would be very glad to jump in an aeroplane to-morrow morning if it were necessary. I trust the parties to the dispute will act not only in their own interests but in the interests of the community and of the dominion as a whole, to assist in the reconstruction of the national economy following the conclusion of the war in the Pacific and in Europe.

maintopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Labour a question supplementary to that asked by my leader? I think I can solve a lot of his difficulties for him. Why not ask the parties to this strike, instead of meeting him in Toronto, to meet him in the Ford offices in Windsor? Then the picket lines are all shot, and he may be able to get these stupid people together so that they can talk to one another.

maintopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext:
I appreciate the constructive suggestion of my hon. friend, but in my opinion, and I say it sincerely, in a

Surplus War Assets

dispute of this description it is far better that we should meet on neutral territory. I am not standing on my dignity or the dignity of a minister of the province of Ontario, but I do not think it is in the best interests of labour relations in this country, looked at from the point of view of either employer or employee, for two ministers to go there and walk through a picket line when one party to the dispute are convinced in their own minds that the attitude taken, the picketing by the union in this instance, is illegal, though they do these things in the United States. That is why I thought Toronto would be the best place.

maintopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext: Surely we are not going to let a thing like that stand in the way of getting this matter settled.

maintopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext: Why not meet in the city hall?

subtopic: DECISIONS OF PREPARATORY COMMITTEE AS TO CHOICE OF HEADQUARTERS

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): On October 4 the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Gray-don), on the orders of the day, asked me certain questions part of which had not been covered by notice he had sent in, and I stated I would get the information and make it available to the house as soon as possible. The question was:
May I ask the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs whether the government has been advised of the decisions taken by the united nations preparatory committee regarding choice of a headquarters for the united nations organization? I ask that question because newspaper reports indicate that the headquarters of that organization is to be situated in the United States. In that connection I make one observation to the minister, namely, that I am not at all satisfied that what I regard as very strong claims for Canada have been pressed as enthusiastically as in my opinion circumstances would warrant.
The answer I wish to make is this. The government has been informed by the Canadian representative on the executive committee of the united nations preparatory commission that, at a meeting on October 3, it was decided by a majority of the executive committee to recommend to the full preparatory commission that the headquarters of the inited nations organization should be in the United States of America. Other locations for the permanent site of the united nations, including more than one site in Canada, had been suggested to the executive committee. According to the reports received from the

Canadian representative, it would appear that, before the recommendation of October 3 was adopted, the choice had narrowed to a selection between a site in a smaller European country, probably Geneva, on the one hand or some location in the United States on the other hand. It is understood that no recommendation has been made as yet by the executive committee as to the place in the United States at which the headquarters might be located.

maintopic: EXPORTS TO THE UNITED STATES DURING LAST SIX MONTHS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: EXPORTS TO THE UNITED STATES DURING LAST SIX MONTHS
speechtext:
On Thursday last the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard) made the following statement and asked a question. I quote from page 758 of Hansard:
Since Canadian canned meats are being advertised for sale by New York city retailers, and being sold free of points, will the government advise the house, at the earliest opportunity, what meats, fresh and canned, have been exported to the United States within the past six months?
The hon. gentleman gave me a copy of an advertisement from a New York paper upon which the question was based. This advertisement indicates that the meat referred to is veal and chicken pate; veal, ham and tongue; beef, pork and ham. These meats are all meat pastes, that is sandwich spreads, and are put up in seven-ounce tins. No permits have been issued for the export of canned meats to the United States in 1945. The figures of the bureau of statistics indicate that during the first six months of this year, 13,200 pounds of fresh beef and 200 pounds of pork were shipped to an army air field in the United States and were not for ordinary domestic use. Canned meat pastes of the type mentioned above have been exported in the amount of 595,407 pounds. There are no meat pastes being exported to the United States, to be sold free of points, which are under ration in Canada at the present time.
On the orders of the day:

I desire to address a question to the Minister of Finance or to the parliamentary assistant to the minister. It is a question relating to meat rationing for repatriated Hong Kong prisoners of war. I gave notice of this question last week. I understand my

Provincial Legislation
colleague from Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) did likewise; therefore I am speaking on his behalf and my own and am duly cognizant of the responsibility. My question, in accordance with that notice, is: will the government consider exempting these Hong Kong repatriates from the meat rationing restrictions, since there is probably a very special need among them, they having had extremely little meat for four years?

speakeroldname: Mr. R. W. MAYHEW (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, notice of the questions of the hon. members for Winnipeg South Centre and Winnipeg South was received too late on Friday to obtain an answer. However, the minister took up with the wartime prices and trade board the question of providing increased quantities of rationed foods to released prisoners from far eastern theatres of war. I am pleased to be able to announce that after consultation with medical officers of the Department of Health and Welfare and the Department of National Defence, it has been decided to issue additional ration coupons covering a period of three months to such released prisoners of war, which will entitle them to a fifty per cent increase in butter and sugar, and one hundred per cent in meat, over the amounts available to the general public. Instructions have been issued to the various ration boards for the issuance of these extra coupons to the released prisoners of war upon application.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the house on Friday last the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked a question as to priorities on building materials, and suggested that I reply to-day. In my remarks of last Friday I find that I have rather confused the issue, and I should now like to make a statement of policy.
In replying on Friday I was anxious to reply to the suggestion by the leader of the opposition that the government should modify its policy because of alleged bottlenecks being created as a result of the priorities in favour of Wartime Housing Limited.
In my reply I was particularly anxious to clear up a popular fallacy about Wartime Housing, namely, that owing to the assistance given to it in building houses for veterans, stocks of building materials are frozen or tied up in warehouses. It is undoubtedly this fallacy which is at the root of the complaints which

have been received by the leader of the opposition and others. I referred at that time to the reports regarding Calgary which on investigation were found to be quite untrue. I might have mentioned the cases of Edmonton and Winnipeg as well, and numerous others, all of which have been investigated and found to be untrue.
In my remarks I stated that there are no building material priorities at all in favour of Wartime Housing Limited. This was not correct. I should have explained that the government is, in fact, giving assistance to Wartime Housing Limited where necessary, and requires producers and distributors in certain cases to deliver to Wartime Housing Limited in priority to other users. The purpose in giving this assistance is to enable Wartime Housing Limited to maintain its building schedule and to complete at the earliest possible time its programme of building the low cost rental houses for veterans which are so urgently required.
The assistance given to Wartime Housing Limited is not a serious factor in creating shortages in materials available to private builders. As I said several days ago, Wartime Housing Limited is building only a very small proportion of the total number of houses under construction at present. To take the case of plumbing supplies, about which the greatest number of complaints have been received, the requirements of Wartime Housing Limited during the last quarter of this year would be less than twenty per cent of the estimated production. Its requirements of other building materials are even smaller, and in some cases will have no effect whatsoever on the supplies available to private builders. In the administration of priorities for Wartime Housing Limited every effort is being made to interfere as little as possible with the normal flow of materials into the building trades. As the production of building materials continues to increase, the government may be able to modify its priority policy as suggested by the leader of the opposition, but for the present it is felt that this is not feasible, since any change is likely to interfere with the building of low rental houses for veterans.

subsubtopic: STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR- STATEMENT OF MR. GILLIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to occupy
any of the time of the house at this stage with the matter I am about to discuss. However, I offer no apologies for doing so because a few days ago I endeavoured to have a brief discussion of this matter, and it might have been settled at that time.
My purpose in rising to-day is to discuss the labour difficulties at Windsor. From time to time the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) can make a statement that suits him in the house, without giving anyone on this side an opportunity of presenting the other side of the question as we understand it. I consider this matter to be of urgent importance; otherwise I would not take the time of the house to discuss it. A few days ago the Minister of Labour, in answer to a question here, referred to the difficulty at Windsor as a siege, and that is what it may very well develop into if steps are not taken to correct the present attitude of the employers, as I understand it. This is not a new matter either to me or to the Department of Labour. The fact is that I raised this question in the house seventeen months ago, and it is exactly the same dispute 47696-53
to-day as at that time, of course with the exception that it has been neglected and pushed aside in the interval, and hopes have been expressed that someone might take a reasonable attitude so that it would not develop into the situation that exists to-day.
While I am discussing this matter as an emergency issue from this side of the house I do not want it understood that I believe no one on the other side has tried to do anything about it. Personally I think some of the members from the area concerned have done everything within their power to have the matter settled in a satisfactory manner; and, as I see it, if the employers were reasonable the matter might have been settled by now.
As I understand it, the situation is this. Here we have our first post-war strike. If the present difficulty is allowed to develop, within the next few months it is likely to culminate in a general strike right across this country. Then, this reflects the inadequacy of th- labour legislation we enacted during the war for the purpose of getting production and improving relations between labour and management. It definitely sets out one thing; that is, that the Ford Motor Company in Windsor and other large employers of labour across this country accepted government legislation during the war because of the pressure of war, but immediately the war was over they took advantage of the loopholes which existed in the labour legislation and cut the line. Now they are back where they were in 1939, with the major objective in mind of defeating any intention the government may have of laying down proper labour legislation which would bring democracy into industry in this country. In other words my conception of the matter is that once again the employers of labour across this country-if the attitude of the Ford Motor Company is the general attitude-have used the workers of this country as suckers in another war; then, as soon as the war is over and the emergency has passed, they are right back where they were in 1939 or 1914. It is because I believe the government should recognize that attitude that I am discussing the matter in the house to-day. It is urgent, because, as was suggested only this afternoon in the house, the packing house workers-an essential group of workers at this time, when we are attempting to feed the people of Europe-are proposing similar action. They are running into exactly the same problems in the packing houses that the Ford workers have run into at Windsor-the fact that the employers want to back up on an agreement and on understandings arrived at during the war.

Ford Motor Plant Strike

Some 30,000 other workers in automobile plants across Canada have already taken strike votes, and to the extent of almost ninety per cent in most of the plants they have decided that when or if the Windsor workers want their assistance in similar action, they are prepared to give that assistance.
Windsor to-day is engaged in a little war, a war that can bring disastrous results to that section of Canada. The issues involved are simple. In 1941 workers at Windsor had signed an agreement with the Ford Motor Company. That agreement carried a clause with respect to grievance procedure, and the manner in which problems of the workers would be relayed to the management. That agreement worked out satisfactorily until May, I believe it was, of 1944, when the Ford Motor Company decided that that grievance procedure arrangement would not be carried on any longer. Because of a slight dispute on that issue the company abrogated the signed agreement and took its present stand. The real issue in Windsor is simply that the workers in that particular plant want to sign an agreement in accordance with the Dominion legislation. They want a union shop; they want some measure of union security, and the check-off for their union dues. That would not cost the Ford Motor Company anything; it is merely a general recognition on the part of the employers and the workers of the right to sit around a conference table, and bargain. That is the main issue.
The question of wages is one which I shall not discuss. As the Minister of Labour has said, that is something to be decided between employers and the union, when or if they decide to sit down together. And may I add this, that the matter of wages as it has been discussed throughout the press, particularly of this province, is most misleading. I have seen the statement in the press to the effect that the Ford workers are demanding a thirty per cent increase in wages. The natural assumption for anyone to make is that the workers are asking that this increase be made on top of their wartime wages. That is not true. We have talked this matter over with officials of the union, and we know the fact is that what they are demanding is a thirty per cent increase on their 1938 rates. The average 1938 wage paid by the Ford Motor Company was between $1,000 and $1,200 a year. The minimum paid in their plant was $600 a year. A thirty per cent increase in basic rates means that the Ford workers are at this time demanding a minimum wage in those plants of $1,800 a year.

In a few minutes I shall be told to take my seat because my time will have expired. However, this question can be discussed by every hon. member in the house after I have finished. Mind you, I am not concerned about simply raising this matter in the house; I want something done about it. Before I take my seat I am going to suggest something that should be done. Whether hon. members are prepared to go along in this matter and see that something is done about it is a test of their sincerity.
As I said a minute ago, I am no-t going to argue wage rates, because there are probably fifty different classifications in that plant -different groups with different rates. But I made that point simply because the press has been misleading.
In 1938 a large percentage of the employees in that plant received $600 a year.

No, no.
How does the hon. member arrive at that-$600 with a thirty per cent increase amounting to $1,800?
But that is not thirty per cent.
A thirty per cent increase in the basic hourly rate would bring them up to that figure per year, as a minimum.

There are many classifications in the Ford plant, as there are everywhere else.

You do not know them,
though.
If I had time I could tell you a lot, if you would take a trip to my office some time.

afternoon.

And howl

As I said a minute ago, the matter of wages is not one I am concerned about. But I am concerned with the matter of establishing the collective agreement, union security and proper bargaining arrangements in the plant-the focal points in this strike.
Let me say this, that it does not reflect any great credit upon the present government in Ontario-because primarily it is their responsibility. If they were accepting that responsibility we would not be discussing the matter in this house this afternoon, and there would be no strike in Windsor.
You had better talk about Nova Scotia.
This could not happen in Nova Scotia. We settled the matter down there thirty years ago.
Well, in Ontario they at least know how much they are getting per hour.
That is the point; I have been trying to tell you. However, if what I say in the house goes over the hon. member's head, that is not my responsibility.
It is pretty evident what the Tory attitude, is anyway.

The minister pointed out that a conference had been called in Ontario, to which union officials and officials of the Ford Motor Company had been invited. If I am correctly informed, the union officials were prepared to go along with that meeting. But the Ford company took the attitude that they were not going to go into any conference with our Department of Labour or with union officials until such time as they and their office workers were permitted to go back into their offices through the picket line. The Minister of Labour in his statement the other day asserted that on that particular point he was in agreement with the Ford Motor Company. I am not going to debate the merits or demerits of the tactics of the workers in keeping out the office staff, but I am going to say this: The office workers are not stopped from going through the picket line. The fact of the matter is that the office workers are not reporting for work. That is our informa-
Ford Motor Plant Strike

tion direct from the union officials, that there is no one stopping the office workers from going through the picket line.
The minister makes quite a play of Mr. Campbell being kept out of his office. The Minister of Labour is an old union man and has taken part in many strikes. A strike is a war, a war between employer and employee, and, the union official has a responsibility to see that that war is conducted in the best interests of those he represents. Mr. Campbell is doing the same thing, and no one is finding fault with him for that. But why does Mr. Campbell want to get back into that office, and why are the Ford workers not much interested in allowing him back into that office? My information is this, and if it is correct, there is justification for what the men are doing, Mr. Campbell has in that plant a lot of blue-prints, a lot of dies and tools, If he could take in fifty or sixty men for a few hours he could gather those up and farm them out to other plants around this province and keep that Ford plant in Windsor closed for the next seven or eight months while he is getting his work done elsewhere, and in the meantime the skilled workers at the Ford plant would be left high and dry. I am not saying that that is a correct analysis, but that is the information we get from union officials in Windsor, and I say that if that is true the workers at Ford have complete justification in keeping Mr. Campbell out of the plant.
Do not forget that Mr. Campbell is the man who started this strike seventeen months ago by his absolutely unreasonable attitude of using the workers once again for a war, and then when the war is over his attitude is: We go back into our little shell and you workers are no longer important in this country. But Mr. Campbell is going to find out before this war is through, as will every other industrialist who takes that attitude, that unless he goes along with his workers in the post-war and establishes the objectives for which we fought this war, he is going to have a very uncomfortable country to live in for the next fifteen or twenty years.
In their efforts to find a solution for the present difficulties the workers at the Ford plant have traversed every piece of machinery that has been provided by the government, all the conciliation machinery, P.C. 1003, every order in council that has been laid down by this government. The workers at the Ford plant have complied with every one of them.
Why does Ford take that attitude in Windsor? The same company, the United States company just across the line, has pro-

vided for its employees in the United States everything that the workers in the Ford plant in Windsor are asking for. Why is there industrial democracy in the United States? Why is not the same union security set up here as there? Why is not the grievance procedure with respect to the stewards that has been provided in the United States for Ford's workers there, provided also in Windsor for Canadian workers? That is something to which the Canadian government has a right to get an answer. There is no reason why the Ford company in Canada should be tying up industry and creating friction by refusing to deal with its employees in this country as it deals with its employees in the United States.
Have they not a million workers out on strike now?
Where?
In the United States.

The question is wages over there. The question here is union security, and that is provided in the United States.
What is the solution? My solution is this, and you have a precedent for it. I do not expect the Minister of Labour to run around all over this country wherever there is a labour dispute; for that is not his job. But he has in his department the necessary machinery and officials that he can direct. I think that what the Minister of Labour should do immediately is to send a controller to Windsor to take over the Ford plant there. If he is prepared to do that the workers at Ford are prepared to go back to the status quo prior to their going out. The Minister of Labour then, through his controller, would try to bring the employer and the employees together to work out an agreement between employer and employee that would be in accordance with the many government pronouncements that have been made in this house on the question of collective bargaining. That is the answer, and it is not something new. This government has already done it. In the middle of the war they took over National Steel Car at Hamilton. There was a strike there, and the Minister of Labour sent in a controller. The strike was settled, and there have been no difficulties there since. The government did the same thing in Montreal in connection with the Montreal Tramways strike last year, where the situation was worse than it is at Windsor now. The Minister of Labour sent in his controller and the difficulties were settled. Just a couple of months ago the Minister of Labour again, when there was a strike in British Columbia in American Can, a company with ramifiea-

Ford Motor Plant Strike
tions all across this continent, sent a controller in there, in a bigger show than this Windsor set-up, and to the best of my knowledge he settled that dispute satisfactorily. The United States government at the present time are not adverse to that line of action. Just a few days ago the United States government stepped into the oil industry in the United States and took over, and is now bringing employer and employee together.
The fact of the matter is that we fought this war for something; hundreds of men left the Ford plant at Windsor to join the armed forces, and now they are coming back and are working in that plant. That is their means of livelihood. We preached to them that in fighting this war they were fighting for democracy, and now they come back to the Ford plant and find that their employer is refusing them the very rudiments of industrial democracy-the right of the employee to bargain with his employer, the right to sign an agreement, the right to say-what their wage rates are to be. Now what will be the opinion of the boy who comes back from fighting this war and finds his employer taking that attitude? It is the same old game that we saw in 1914-18. We fought a war from 1939 to 1945, and now the war is over, and the war slogans are down. Personally the war is not over for me, and it is not over for the hundreds of thousands of young men who are coming back to this country after fighting a war that they really thought they were fighting for democracy.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that in a situation such as this, where there is a dispute, the first one in the post-war period that can affect labour relations clear across this country, the responsible government should step in through the Department of Labour and see to it that a sensible understanding is arrived at, based on the principles which were often enunciated by the Minister of Labour and other members of the government on the subject of labour relations during the process of fighting the war.
My hon. friend over here was much concerned about the question of wages, and I said that I was not going to go into that because it is not my business; it is the business of Ford and the employees when they come together. But let me leave this thought with you, if you think that the wage demands which the employees are making at this time are unreasonable. I understand from fairly good authority that during the years of the war the Ford Motor Company, Canadian section, made $27 million profits after all taxes were paid; they increased their reserves from $60 million to $90 million; they paid dividends

to shareholders of $9 million. I understand that if two and a half million dollars were taken from that $30 million of reserves they put away during the process of fighting this war and were applied to the dispute now going on at Windsor, it would settle the whole question. The company would still have a lot of money.
What does the hon. member mean, that two and a half million dollars would settle the whole question?
It would provide for the increases in wages.
For how long?
For a year.
And after the year was up, what then?
Take some more out of the $90 million reserve.
That is all right, but explain that.
We can see where their friends are.
Ford's friends are very obvious in this house.
No, not "Ford's friends"; but we are not going to be deluded by a one-sided argument.

I shall not detain the house any longer. I feel very strongly on this matter, and I seriously suggest to the Minister of Labour and every hon. member that action should be taken by the department immediately to head off what I consider to be the initial stages of a general industrial upheaval in this country if the dispute is not handled at once and in a reasonable manner.

I believe the workers of this
country are puzzled, dismayed and discouraged at the lack of a positive labour policy on the part of the government. We can remember that up to June 11 they had a policy-jobs, work for all, security for all. Where is that policy now? The workers at Windsor are without protection, and surely the most elementary protection for the workers in a democracy is the right to join the union of their own choice, the protection of union security, the closed shop, and the check-off. Yet these are being denied to them, and apparently the government does nothing about it. Well, I believe either the government's promises are going to be ful-

filled, or their bluff is going to be called, because the insecurity of labour is becoming more and more obvious.
All across this country to-day men are being laid off; plants all over Canada are reducing their staffs. I draw to the attention of the house the fact that when a man is laid off or when he is on strike it is a very serious matter for that individual. There are few scourges worse than unemployment. When a man is unemployed he has no income. It is true that to-day he gets this miserly pittance of unemployment insurance, but that is far from adequate to pay his rent, it is far from adequate to provide food, including the dairy products which are so necessary to keep his children in health; it is far from adequate to provide medical services if they are needed; it is far from adequate in these days of approaching winter to see that the house is kept properly warm and that the children do not suffer. Always under strikes or mass unemployment it is the children who suffer most. Therefore I suggest that there is much validity to our case and to the union case that when the worker is being transferred from war-time to peace-time employment, during the period of transition he should be given a minimum of $25 a week. He and his family cannot expect to live on less.
Under capitalism as we have known it the lot of the worker has been unemployment, then work for a little time, then unemployment again. There is no security. In our lifetime we have gone through two wars and two major depressions, and the mass of the people have always suffered the worst. There are young men coming back to this country whose only chance in the nineteen thirties was the chance in 1939 to fight and die for Canada, These boys are coming back expecting something better than when they went away. They want a Canada wherein there is work for them, and some sort of union security, but apparently the government is unwilling to provide that type of security. In Winnipeg we have the case of MacDonald Brothers Aircraft plant, which at the peak of employment had 4,500 men employed. The number is now down to 400. What has happened to those 4,100 people? Some, though only a few, have got other jobs; some have left the province; the great majority are unemployed.
I want again to emphasize the fact that unemployment is a personal tragedy for those who suffer from it, and therefore, it is the duty of the government and this house to do everything within their power to ease con-
ditions for these people and see that the pledges are kept that there shall be work for all in Canada.
We are told that there are a million new jobs in sight. Where are they, and at what rates of pay? I believe that the "million new jobs" is a mirage. It does not delude the workers of this country. It is true that there may be a million new jobs, but if there are, they are at twenty-five cents an hour, and we are not going to take them at that wage.

If the government are to be sure of getting the support of the working people of this country, they have to support-

They want to make sure that we do not go back to prewar wage levels and insecurity. They are not there fighting merely for the Ford employees but for the men who are coming back from overseas and who will not be satisfied to go back to pre-war conditions.
The strike is not something that these workers have brought about because they wanted to strike. It is not that. Workers in various plants and industries have felt for the past year a change in the attitude of employers. Before V-E day, when war materials were necessary, employers were willing to collaborate, but once they felt that the war was coming to an end they started to provoke trouble in the shops. They laid off active unionists and fired certain workers and rehired at lower wages. All these methods were resorted to in order to prepare for the post-war period. The workers to-day on strike are saying that this is not going to happen. If their income is insufficient it will not be merely the Ford workers who will suffer. What about the storekeeper, the dentist, the doctor, and everyone else?
We have been speaking in government documents about high income; that is mentioned in most government documents. But how will anyone obtain a high income unless the government gives the lead by encouraging an increase in wages? I should like to know what sort of increase has there been in the productivity of labour in industry. According to certain figures I have seen, it appears that there has been an increase of thirty per cent in industrial efficiency in the United States. I do not know what the corresponding increase in productivity in Canada has been, but I believe there has been a similar increase. Thus an increase in wages for Canadian labour will not affect profits. In fact, I have no doubt that when it comes to profit*

I was very much disappointed in the replies I received last week from the Minister of Labour regarding steps to settle the Ford strike. I was told about a home being one's castle. I did not know that the office was Mr. Campbell's home, although I understand he has built up very elaborate offices in the plant. I should have liked to hear some word of encouragement from the Minister of Labour rather than the statement that he thought the other party was right. In my opinion P.C. 1003 should be amended, and it should be amended in such a way that Campbell will know that he must meet with the union; that union security is the law of the land. I have met many boys who have come back from overseas. What do they say? They have been flying officers, flight-lieutenants, lieutenants in the army and so on. They have got used to a new standard of living, and they will insist upon a decent standard when they get back.
The union is fighting for these boys just as much as for the small storekeeper. These people are fighting for every worker in the country and they should get the support of this government. It is not enough for the
(Mr. Rose.]

Mr. Speaker, when I listened in this house some weeks ago to a discussion as to whether this august assembly should declare the war at an end or whether we should wait some months before the Canadian government put its stamp of approval on the fact that peace had come to this land, even though our armed forces had ceased fighting the enemy, I was at a loss to know why we should be debating that problem. Hon. gentlemen to my immediate right kept insisting that the war should be declared over, because then the process of removing controls might get under way, which would give certain interested persons an opportunity to get back into free enterprise on a proper and unrestricted scale. First I suspected that possibly the war controls instituted by the government during the last five years were being retained to bring about an orderly transition from war to peace, as was indicated by a number of hon. members on the other side of the house. Then in reading various press reports relating to strikes in British Columbia, at Toronto, at Guelph and at Windsor, with the rumblings of a strike at Winnipeg; seeing the. football being thrown from the provincial government to the Minister of Labour at Ottawa and back; seeing the Minister of Labour here step into a reportedly provincial matter and settle the American Can strike in British Columbia by forcing a board of conciliation on the two disputants; seeing that when the packing house employees all across Canada were on strike or in process of going on strike the Ontario Minister of Labour took up the cudgel and was able to settle a dominion dispute, as a novice in this house 
I was left definitely at sea as to who had jurisdiction in any given field of labour legislation.
Might I say to my hon. friend that he is still at sea, though I regret having to say so.
Just a minute, now.
All right; an attack is being made on myself and on the Ontario Minister of Labour, who is not here.
I made no attack on the Minister of Labour of Ontario. I said he settled a strike which was of dominion-wide proportions.
That is a different-thing. First you said it was a dominion affair.

I did not make a deliberate attack on the Ontario Minister of Labour. I am quite happy that he settled the dispute in question, though I did not say so.
Coming back to the point I was trying to make when the Minister of Labour corrected me on my way of expressing my opinions in this matter, we have certain wartime labour controls. As I see it, if we had to have those controls at all they should have been allinclusive. Apparently some government, whether it be the Tory government at Toronto or our own government here at Ottawa, is able under certain conditions to step in and either by conciliation or by an enforced arbitration, as happened in the two cases I mentioned, settle a labour dispute, under powers vested in the government by certain war measures and orders in council. I have come to the conclusion that the power of the government of this country is being used not to force reasonable conciliation in these disputes but to keep wages frozen, to keep overtime pay frozen, to keep minimum hours of labour frozen at a maximum figure. In my own province of Saskatchewan, where the provincial government authorized two weeks' vacation with pay for all employees, the power of the federal government was invoked to prevent those employees from receiving the holidays to which they were justly entitled. Only this afternoon I was reading in the Labour Gazette something relating to P.C. 9384, which is the wartime wages control order, in which various judgments of regional labour boards were given to this effect: "the primary function of war labour boards is to stabilize the wage structure in Canada, and that purpose cannot be achieved by equalizing wages across the various economic regions of Canada."

So we have restrictive measures still in operation and being skilfully used by employers who request their application by the government because otherwise there will be an upward revision of the wage structure as a result of which the prices of commodities will go up. These restrictions are in effect in spite of the fact that the workers of this country are in a fatigued condition as the result of long hours with little if any overtime pay. This situation was emphasized to me two years ago at Dagenham, Essex, when I happened to be the luncheon guest of the managing director for England of the Ford Motor Company. I did not discuss politics on that occasion, or I might not have been given this reply to a question I asked with respect to worker fatigue. Mr. Cooper, managing director of Ford at Dagenham, said that in the plants of his company, owing to the excessive hours workers were employed because of the need for producing all available munitions of war, and because of the extra hours that were entailed in roof watching, home guard duties and so on, the incidence of accidents was increasing and the precision of the work being done was decreasing. This being so, if employers are interested in the efficiency of their plants it would seem to me that from that point of view, if for nothing else,* they would accede to the demands of their employees without having to be threatened with a strike. I will say to the credit of most employers of labour in this country that in spite of the restrictions on giving two weeks' holidays with pay each year, many of them have voluntarily recognized the necessity of their people having these holidays.

The government, working in the first instance through the Department of Reconstruction, is making plans to meet these local situations. of Reconstruction simply reiterates that there will be a more or less continuously high rate of employment, high income for the workers, social security and, I had hoped, collective bargaining. I could go on ad infinitum-or possibly I should say ad nauseam.
In my home city of Regina the problem of reconversion of our major industrial plant, Regina Industries, was settled rapidly. No more than a week after election day, quit slips were being handed out to the employees at the rate of roughly 150 per week. This was done to a point where, to-day, the one large industrial plant in our city is operating only on a skeleton-staff basis. The potentialities of the plant for any form of industrial production are going to be lost to western Canada, and therefore to the country as a whole because, as I understand from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott), the building is to be turned over for use as an ordnance depot.
The people in that plant who had developed certain skills did not go on strike, nor did they have the opportunity to do so. They were simply eased out because there was no work for them. The manufacture of Bren gun tripods for the Chinese government, which has been proceeding in the plant since June, is one of the outstanding jokes in our war production- simply because those tripods are obsolete. At any rate, the men and women who were working in that plant now have the option of either accepting work offered them at points outside Regina, or accepting unemployment insurance -and ultimately, of course, relief. It is not a simple matter to root up an entire family in one of the prairie provinces and move it either to eastern Canada or to British Columbia for the work obtainable in those areas. Selective service assured our workers in Regina that work was available at those points.
The acceptance of unemployment insurance offers no great incentive to the average citizen. In my view the Unemployment Insurance Act passed in 1940 is an iniquitous piece of legislation. We find that out of approximately 5,000,000 persons gainfully employed, 2,500,000 are covered by the terms of this legislation. The act is full of loopholes. Contributions must be made to the fund for 180 days by an employee in the two years immediately preceding an application for unemployment insurance benefits. To receive those benefits the individual concerned must be capable of and available for work, and must be unable to obtain suitable employment. In other words, he must be capable of earning. But if, through no fault of his own, a man

becomes sick, the act is not worth the snap of a finger, because under this legislation sickness is a bar to the receipt of benefits.
I did not like the implication of the hon. member who immediately preceded me in the debate, when he said that those of us in this group who are drawing attention to the seriousness of the situation are thereby aggravating its seriousness. But may I point out that those who are now on strike, by the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act are ineligible for receipt of benefits, because strikers are barred from participation.
Moreover, no insurance benefits are available for the first nine days of unemployment in any benefit year. I know the employees of this country are not Mahatma Ghandis; they cannot enter upon nine-day hunger strikes, when conditions develop which would cause those strikes. This is another principle which deters our working people from making the final and serious move of taking strike action. The very fact that the workers at Windsor are on strike, after seventeen months of negotiation, and after exploring every available channel to secure redress for what they considered to be their grievances signifies clearly to me that their action is definitely that of a last resort.
Another serious defect in the Unemployment Insurance Act, to which I would draw the attention of the house, is that section of the Act which states that if a worker leaves employment without just cause, or is discharged for cause, he is not eligible for benefits.
The solvency of the fund, as set out in section 79, is something which will have to have the attention of hon. members in the very near future. Figures I have, show that in 1942 there were 26,900 applications filed for benefits under the act. In 1943 that number had risen to 36,600 and in 1944 to 30,897. In the first six months of this year the number of applications was 76,821, almost equal that of the whole of 1944. These were the applications for benefits which paid to married men with dependents, if acceptable under the Unemployment Insurance Act, a minimum of $1.80 and up to a maximum of $14.40 per week. These are the figures regardless of the number of dependents.
From the point of view of solvency, the defect in the fund as it is set up under section 79 is that no provision is made for continuity of payments to the fund. I do not wish to indulge in carping criticism, because as a matter of fact I think the government should be congratulated upon having instituted the semblance of an unemployment insurance

fund, even though it follows belatedly the example of other enlightened countries throughout the world. But there are so many loopholes in the Unemployment Insurance Act that either when the workers call upon its benefits they cannot get them, or the $300 million at present in the fund will soon be exhausted.
I have one more reference to make before sitting down. A friend drew my attention to the dominion government telephone directory for the month of May, and in that directory I find listed under various departments of government, 1,582 telephone numbers of army officers: 9 lieutenant-generals or major-generals; 23 brigadiers; 75 colonels; 175 lieutenant-colonels; 335 majors; 613 captains; only 352 lieutenants, or second-lieutenants. That makes a grand total of 1,582 brass hats, shall we say. I was in service, Mr. Speaker; I was an officer wearing His Majesty's uniform; but when I think of the intricate mess in which the business of this country becomes entangled because scattered around various government buildings in the city of Ottawa there are enough officers to staff adequately three fighting Canadian divisions overseas, I am appalled. I do not think that all these brass hats so-called are from the province of Saskatchewan either. Even that might require some closer checking up. I have an idea also that the air force and the navy are adequately represented.
We are looking after certain people in this transition period. Certain parts of the army, as I say, are well represented. I have an idea, without knowing the actual facts, that these 1.582 telephone numbers of army officers in the May directory of the government cannot be matched by an equal number of telephones for privates and non-commissioned officers. But certain people are being provided for in this rehabilitation period while the workers of this country, who also did their bit, get the runaround. I would urge upon the Minister of Labour, for the sake of peace, order and good government in this fair Dominion of Canada, that he step into this strike at Windsor just as he stepped in to settle the labour dispute in the American Can Company in British Columbia.
