Ford Motor Plant Strike
which happens to be the reason why the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) brings this matter to the attention of the house. Its significance is that that strike is just the beginning of a process which, if labour does not hinder it, will go on until wages have dropped to the point at which they were before the war, and it is because labour is determined to resist that and because they recognize that the power of their union, which implies collective bargaining, is the only weapon they can use to resist it, that you have the strike at Windsor. That, sir, is why there will be many more strikes in the next five years if something is not done about it. So, while some hon. members think this is not the time and not the place to bring this matter up-I have heard that said for many years in this house-I do not know of any better time and I know of no better place to talk about this matter than here and now. True, we tried to talk about it at some other time, but we were not given the opportunity. This is the only other chance afforded by the rules of the house for us to present something at least of the case of the workers at the Ford plant at Windsor.
I am not going to offer any sharp criticism of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). I recognize that his job, if I may call it such, is a very difficult one, not only in this but in all similar disputes. His department, unfortunately for him, happens to be that point at which both the employers and employees meet in their conflict, and as such he has the most difficult task of perhaps any minister of the crown. I would suggest that the government should give him greater assistance by putting behind him a better policy, a policy which he can carry out with his whole heart, and which will be in line with what we might expect in a. country that has fought for and won democracy.
I would, however, suggest to the Minister of Labour that it does seem to me to be almost bringing this matter to an absurdity to say that action cannot be taken because Mr. Campbell cannot get into his office. I am not going to attempt any defence of the action which prevents him, other than to say that in my view, according to my information, the keeping of the workers out of their offices has now become a point of importance to the strikers. That is a factor in the case, but I do not believe that action on the strike by the minister should be delayed because of a minor point of that kind.
I agree most heatily with the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) that the minister should exercise whatever power he has and call the important leaders together, both of the industry concerned and of the striking men, and try to settle the difficulty-and forget about Mr. Campbell's office.
The government, I insist, must do something about this. Not only is the strike at Windsor the beginning of a struggle which, as I have said, will go on until wages drop to a point where the greatest possible profits can be made in peace time-that is the tendency- but it must not be forgotten that an essential industry, no matter which it is, has vital contacts with the whole industrial system of the nation. I would say to the Minister of Labour and to the government that it is just as important for the well-being of the nation and for the people involved in this strike that industry should be kept going in peace time as it was kept going in war. That is something the government will have to learn. True, it endeavoured to maintain full production during the war, and although it may not always have completely reached that objective it made a very creditable job. I suggest that the responsibility still rests on the government to perform that function.
It is being argued by influential people in Canada to-day that we cannot maintain wartime wages and war-time prices. It has been suggested by some of our influential newspapers that the time has come for this parliament and for the government to face up to that issue. One editorial remarks that, "what does seem to be suggested is a matter of common sense, and it is that either prices should be adjusted to wages or wages to prices." But mark this: "To leave the matter to a scuffle in the dark between labour and capital hardly seems sensible." That is precisely what this government is doing, in the case not only of Windsor but of the entire industrial system. They are leaving wage workers to scuffle with their employers in the dark in an attempt to maintain their wages at a living standard. The figures with respect to the wages of the striking workers in Windsor have been given by the hon. member who introduced this discussion. I need not repeat them, beyond laying emphasis upon the lowest figure he quoted, that of $600 a year as an income for the head of a family, which was included in an average wage which reached from $1,000 to $1,200 a year. Every hon. member knows that even $1,200 is not sufficient for a full life in Canada to-day, and we ought to be prepared to do something about it. Further, every one of us knows, if we know anything
Ford Motor Plant Strike

about this situation or any similar one, that collective bargaining is the only instrument which labour so far has been able to use effectively in raising its wages when wages began to go down.
I add my voice in support of the suggestion already made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that the government should send in a controller to keep this industry going while the processes of reaching agreements are continued. That would be a good way to get into Mr. Campbell's office; let a government controller go there and I am quite sure that he will be admitted through the picket lines. That will remove the difficulty, and the minister can then proceed to his heart's content to settle the strike.
I have said that the Minister of Labour should have a government policy behind him in a matter of this kind. Of course he has, but I imagine it is a policy he cannot like very well. I cannot imagine, from his background, his knowledge, and his fights for labour, that he is particularly happy there. I cannot imagine any labour man being particularly happy as a labour minister in any government which stands for the status quo, and I know the present minister must have his difficulties in that environment.
This government stands for free private enterprise. Now free private enterprise is manifesting its capacity to meet the industrial requirements of this nation from one coast to the other at the present moment. It has entirely failed to prevent vast numbers of men from being laid off without any income except the $14 a week which they may get if and when they receive their unemployment insurance. Free private enterprise has failed to meet the situation in Windsor. Free private enterprise is dabbling away with the problem in the packing plants until the first thing we know we shall have a strike at Winnipeg, Vancouver and other points, tying up the whole live stock industry. Free private enterprise has failed so badly that in the last two weeks we have had, to my knowledge, at least three deputations from various parts of Canada interviewing or seeking to interview the government with respect to the failures of free private enterprise to meet their immediate requirements. We had, for instance, a delegation of 300 in this building a short time ago. They had a specific programme, and their whole plea was that free private enterprise was failing to meet the situation. We had a delegation from Prince Rupert and other parts of British Columbia having to do particularly with rehabilitation and the transition period from war to peace-time industry.

We had another deputation from greater British Columbia centring, I (believe, in Vancouver and Victoria. These three different deputations inside of the last two weeks, along with threatened strikes which I have mentioned and the strike of which we are now speaking, indicate that in so short a time after the cessation of hostilities free private enterprise is on its knees. But it is part of the business of free private enterprise to allow the lag to come so that wages may be forced down, in order that greater profits may be assured for it in the future.
Therefore I am very sorry indeed that the minister has not a policy which would enable -him to meet, and meet satisfactorily, a situation of this kind, a policy which would guarantee every possible assistance to industry in order that it might function as a service to all the people of Canada.
I know pretty well what the government policy about industry is, as I have gathered it from its own published statements. I believe its policy is to allow free private enterprise to have free play until it becomes absolutely imperative for the government to do something, and this means that we shall have perhaps hundreds of thousands of people unemployed and perhaps riots here and there. Then the government is supposed to do something, and what it will do then is to increase public expenditures on public works to take up the slack. According to my information, that is the government's policy. Let free private enterprise carry on until it sticks, as the government is quite sure it will; when it actually does stick, then the government will make expenditures, and those expenditures are to be made from borrowed money, with interest to be paid on the borrowed money, so that the people have to pay higher taxes in order to pay the higher interest to the money-lenders. And so goes our system, like a snake that starts to eat its own tail, until it gets to the back of its neck and cannot go farther. That is the kind of economic system we now have in this country. The snake is busy eating its tail now and it will not be long coming up through the body.
I want to suggest one or two things to the government, knowing of course

well, at least hopeful that they will act immediately on them.
You should have fired the first barrel. I think I know what you were going to say.
I want to point out first of all that we have fought for democracy, but I wonder whether as a parliament we have ever made any effort to say what this means, to

Ford Motor Plant Strike
say whether a wage of $600 a year is fit for anyone in a democracy for which young men died. I wonder if we have ever tried to visualize what this thing means for which our men have given their lives. A country that cannot provide homes for its people calling itself a democracy! A country that can find neither jobs for its people nor sufficient income to maintain a standard of decent living calling itself a democracy! I feel about this, as I am quite sure many hon. members feel, that these young men have made a tremendous sacrifice for democracy, and I am damned if I am going to stand here and watch it made a fool of by this government or any other government.
I want to see the people of Canada get democracy. I want to see them get democracy in industry; I want to see them get democracy in ownership of the means by which they live; I want to see them get democracy in the ruling of their industrial lives and pursuits; I want to see the workers have a share in 'he policies of industry, in what they are making, how it is to be made, and all the conditions of labour. I want to see democracy in reality.
That is the fight which is beginning. The fight for democracy has been fought on the military field. The fight now swings into the political and industrial field; as it swings in there I swing in behind it, and so do all of us in this group. And these men are merely the first to make a protest.
I want the government then to guarantee first of all-a very small thing-a minimum income of $25 a week or $100 a month to every worker in Canada between his employment as a war worker and the time he is engaged in similar occupation in peace pursuits, and I want to see at the same time that that becomes a basic wage below which no worker in Canada will be permitted to work in the days that are to come. That is the first thing.
I know the question of money will be raised as usual. I have listened for days to the discussion of a money bill in this house and hon. members, particularly to my right, have laid stress on the enormous amounts of money we hav been spending, how much more we are spending now than we spent twenty years ago. Who cares whether we are spending more now? If we were not spending more now than twenty years ago we would be fit only for a lunatic asylum. The point is, can we produce the goods? That is the first point, and the second point is, can the people of this country consume them? You may say, no; they cannot consume them all. All right; let us fill them up anyhow. Let us fill them up once; let us put something on their backs once; let
us give them a home once; let us see to it that all the people of Canada have all they can eat of wholesome food, that they have homes in which to live, homes that are comfortable, beautiful and worthy of a democracy. Let us see that their children have a chance at education and that they have an opportunity to maintain a free life. Let us do these things; then what is left over we can use for foreign trade, and I imagine there will be quite a bit left over. But let us make sure that our people are not going to be deprived of anything that can- be produced in Canada whiLe machinery and workers are idle and material is going to waste. That is the business of government. That is the responsibility of this administration; the administration is going to be held to that responsibility, and this strike is the first sign of its task.
I suggest to the minister, therefore, that he do two things: first, that he call the leaders together and, if he cannot effect a settlement immediately, he put a controller in there in the interests of government until the matter is settled. I advocate this not particularly for the strikers of Windsor but as an industrial policy for the future. We cannot afford to tie up any great industry in a country in which the people need goods, and it is the business of government to see that our industries are kept going and that those who labour in them receive sufficient for their labours to make it possible for them to live democratically; that is, to live in accordance with a standard of living for which they would not be ashamed that their fighting men overseas had died.

We all agree, I believe, with the objectives which have been expressed by our C.C.F. friends. I believe we all agree with the fine sentiments expressed by the previous speaker (Mr. Irvine). I am quite sure that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) agrees with all that. I rather suspect that ninety-five per cent of the Liberal party agrees with it. But the big problem which confronts them is, where is the money coming from to do all this?
You tell us.

That is what I rose to do. During the ten years I have been in this house I think I have never found fault with a difficulty without offering a possible solution, and I propose to make no exceptions to that rule. Whether the people who listen to me will have vision and understanding sufficient to be able to appreciate the solution I offer is a matter for their concern, not for mine.

We shall try.
Ford Motor Plant Strike

May I point out to all hon. members something of the problem which confronts the labouring man not only in the Ford plant at Windsor but throughout the length and breadth of this country. In a few minutes I am going to read a statement from the bureau of statistics which conveys a doleful picture of the wage situation which prevailed in Canada in 1941. First of all, let me give a summary of that finding. During the twelve months period which ended on June 2, 1941, of the Canadian wage-earners 32-9 per cent received less than 8450 a year. How many of my Conservative friends want to see the boys come home from overseas and go into jobs where they get as little as that? How many of my Liberal friends want to see that? The next question is, what are you ready to do about it? Do you not realize that the system you are operating to-day, against which these Ford workers are striking, is the very same system that in four years will force the labour people of Canada back into that wage structure? What about it? Do you want that? What are you going to do about it?
In the year ended June 2, 1941, 28-7 per cent of the wage-earners of Canada received between $450 and $949 a year. Now, my Conservative friends, how many of you want to see your boys return from overseas and take that wage? How many of you Liberals want to see your boys take that wage? Yes, but suppose it is your boy; that is a different matter altogether. Suppose it is you, then what? How would you like to try to support a wife and three or four children on a wage like that?
These men in this Ford plant realize that those conditions actually did prevail; they actually lived through them. The members of this house sat and twiddled their idle, useless thumbs while it went on, and the Liberal government under the charge of William Lyon Mackenzie King sat there and allowed them to do it. These are extremely serious matters.
Furthermore, 29-9 per cent of all the wage-earners in Canada received in that same year between $950 and $1,949 a year. I should like to ask how many members of this house want to see the boys they raised and saw go overseas come back and take that wage? This adds up to the following impressive total: In the year ending June 2, 1941, a war year, 91-5 per cent of the wage-earners of Canada were receiving under $1,950 a year. Before we can fully appreciate the ardour and the fervour and determination with which these men in the Ford plant are waging their battle with every means at their command, we must understand the gloom of the picture which they see,

and get their point of view. And when we understand it, let us get our newspaper supporters all over this country to give that picture so that everybody understands it. I have the idea that the members of this house can have considerable influence on the newspapers, especially where these members happen to be Liberals and Conservatives.
It is of the first importance that the Canadian people be informed as to the true facts which obtain in this country. Let us take a look at the case of the Ford Motor company owners. We must understand both sides. Let us see what confronts them. But before we do have a discussion on their problem, let us ask ourselves this question. Why did those wage rates prevail in Canada? Tell me, am I right when I say that those wage rates prevailed in Canada because of a foreign trade complex which exists in the minds of the Canadian people? If I am wrong I shall welcome being corrected by any Liberal or Conservative who will produce evidence to prove his point.
When we are labouring under the foreign trade complex we naturally assume, if we are employers, that wages must come down because prices must come down, because we must be able to sell our goods in competition with other producers, first of all in our own country, and second, in other countries, producing goods that will compete with our goods in foreign markets. That is argued by producers. That puts the employers, perhaps not the Ford motor people to so great an extent, but certainly the packing people and most other producers, in an almost impossible position. Their backs, too, are to the wall. Each side in this struggle finds itself with its back to the wall; each feels that it must fight to protect its very existence; each adopts whatever weapons and tactics it considers essential to success. Thus we see the struggle in Windsor to-day threatening our very national peace, order and good government, if not ultimately our very national existence.
Our C.C.F. friends will say, well, it is an evidence that private enterprise has failed. I say that is pure piffle. It is not evidence that private enterprise has failed. It is evidence that private enterprise is thoroughly alert, thoroughly familiar with the situation confronting it, and is fighting to subsist. If it is unable to make a success of the situation it is not an evidence that private enterprise is failing; it is an evidence that government policy in this country is failing; it is an evidence that we are endeavouring to make work a system which cannot possibly work.

Ford Motor Plant Strike
The thing that nearly everyone in the debate thus far has condemned in the government is this attitude which I, too, condemn, namely, that the government seems to take the position that the government is merely a referee in the situation; that the government must not participate in this quarrel between these little boys; that it is not responsible in the situation. I will not say that the minister has taken the attitude that he is not responsible, but thus far his attitude has been such that he appears to take the view that somebody else must take the responsibility before he can assume his.
Now may I say this once more. The government will simply have to change its financial system or this kind of thing will go on to the ultimate utter destruction of the country. Already we can see what may happen. The government never will be able to solve the problems under the present system. When I say we must change the system, I do not mean that we must change to government ownership, and I will discuss that for a moment or two shortly. I do not want to quarrel with my C.C.F. friends, but I wish to tell them that in my judgment they are barking up the wrong tree; they are going up a blind alley. If they were to apply their policies in this country they would not succeed any better than the present system is succeeding, because they would not be putting their finger on the main cause of the trouble.
The present system distributes too little purchasing power, and it cannot do otherwise. Let us for a moment refer to the figures I used a short time ago. If enterprise, whether government or private, in this country were obliged to compete in the foreign market, certainly it would have to bring down the prices of its goods in order to go on that foreign market. What would it do? That is a matter which has to be considered very carefully. Let us look again at the figures I gave. It will be noticed that I pointed out that 91-5 per cent of all the wage-earners of Canada were receiving less than $1,950, and 32-9 per cent of them were receiving less than $450. In a country where the wage-earners are getting such meagre incomes as those, how in the world can the Ford Motor Company or Canada Packers or any other organization sell its goods? That is the first difficulty. There just is not the purchasing power going into the hands of the people to enable them to buy the goods. And if all the industries in the country were taken over by the government and run as government concerns, that fact would not necessarily change the wage structure one
dollar. If the wage structure were raised, then unquestionably the prices of goods would rise and the problem of selling the goods would be accentuated and intensified. The fact that under our present system insufficient purchasing power is consistently going into the hands of the people puts private enterprise under an impossible handicap; and to blame private enterprise for inability to deal with the situation confronting us is as bad as to tie a man hand and foot, weigh him down with a hundred pound weight, and blame him because he is not able to run. Under the present financial system private enterprise has not the ghost of a chance. There must be a means of obtaining purchasing power which can be distributed among the people, which can increase the incomes of those people whose wages we have had under review.
Even if the government owned the plants the same thing would be true. I believe the average run of our C.C.F. people and a great many of the socialistically inclined people in the Liberal party, the Conservative party and elsewhere, as well as throughout the country, have in mind an idea with regard to the profits people are making that is altogether fallacious. There are big profits in some cases, yes; but any man who has ever taken over even a farm and tried to make a go of it-
Or a brick yard.

-yes, or a brickyard, and tried to make a go of it, or any kind of concern, knows how hard it is to make profits. As I look over my C.C.F. friends, I do not know how many of them have ever tried to do that. It is hard to make profits and easy to lose them in just a few bad years. By way of example, in a perfectly kindly way, may I suggest that for a moment we consider what would happen if the C.C.F. were in power in Canada and took over the Ford plant. I should like to ask three or four questions. Let us ask them in a perfectly straightforward way, because we must have the truth. Would they pay all the workers a living wage?
Yes.

I imagine all the
members of the C.C.F. would chorus yes, as their leader has done. Would that living wage be less than $1,800 a year? I do not think any member of the C.C.F. would dare say no.
I would say it could not be less.

You would not say it could be less, would you? .
Ford Motor Plant Strike
No.
You would not consider for a moment having a wage of less than $1,800 a year?
I do not think a man can live decently on less than that if he is married.

I quite agree. You see, social crediters and the C.C.F. do not disagree very much (with respect to objectives; it is when we come to techniques that we disagree. Now, this is the question the C.C.F. would have to answer immediately. Where would the money come from with which to give those workers $1,800 a year? They would say, out of profits.
Out of production, not out of profits.
Well, you could not possibly get it out of production without taking it out of profits.
Would you let me answer that question for you?
Yes, gladly.
My answer is that we would not hesitate to create just as much money as was necessary to equal the goods we were competent to produce.
I am very glad to hear that answer, and I presume it meets with the approval of the leader of the party; is that right?
That is right.

Then I am going to ask the C.C.F. why they have been so busy for years now trying to destroy the social credit movement in Canada, which is the one movement which has gone on record as favouring that very thing. Now let them explain that.
No; you have the cart before the horse.
That is a pretty weak answer.
Maybe we are getting together now.

If we do it is the C.C.F. who will have to do the getting together, because they are wrong. If they agree with what the hon. member for Cariboo has just said, then no member of the C.C.F. has any right whatever to oppose any social erediter in this country; he could not in honour do so, because that is precisely the attitude the social credit, people have taken.
Then why did the social crediters disapprove the hon. member for Cariboo in 1935?

If I remember correctly the hon. member for Cariboo had a rather bad record when he got out to Alberta in 1935. He did most excellent work in the House of Commons; he made some speeches of which any social erediter would be proud, but when he went to Alberta later he rather spoiled it all. But we will discuss that later on; I think we have the goods on my hon. friend which will be quite sufficient if we have to use them.
If the C.C.F. favour the creation of money to equal the goods produced, that is fine. Why have they not advocated it in this house up to this time? They have never done so. Probably now they are beginning to favour that idea. I think you will find, Mr. Speaker, as the days go by in this country, that all parties, perhaps the C.CF. first, will come to realize that the one group which was right in this matter in 1935 was the Social Credit group. They will find that the social crediters were right in their monetary views; that they were right in their price views; that they were right in their dividend views. Why, the C.C.F. even advocate a dividend of $25 a week; that was done by the hon. member who just preceded me. Other parties will find that the social crediters were right in their war ideas and in every single thing upon which they made a public pronouncement.
And will be right in days to come.

And you will find that the members of the other groups gradually will come to that point of view. If the Canadian people could only know that this would happen quickly enough to save us from disasters which threaten, such as the Ford dispute, then the people could breathe a sigh of relief.
There just is no possible way of solving this problem except the way I suggest. I ask this: Where would the money come from? If the C.C.F. would use the method that the social crediters suggest, use the price system they suggest, use the wage system they suggest and use the dividend system they suggest; in other words, if the C.C.F. would become social crediters, they would solve the problem. And they would find that if they did that they would not need to own the plants. All they would have to do with the Ford Motor Company is this-and I hope the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) will not make any silly mis-

Ford Motor Plant Strike
takes because he has made many in this House of Commons. He had better not laugh a foolish laugh until he realizes that if the Ford Motor Company knew its prices would be guaranteed by social credit technique: if it knew positively that its workers would be guaranteed their incomes by social credit technique, and if the workers knew that their incomes would be guaranteed by that technique, and that markets for their goods would be guaranteed by that same social credit technique, they would end the strike to-night. There would be no further argument at all. There would be no need for any government to take over the plant.
Where could one find an organization more efficient in the building of motor cars than is the Ford Motor Company? For what do hon. members suppose the company is operating its plant? Is it just for fun? Does anyone imagine for a split second they would not sell their goods, all the goods they can possibly manage to make, if they could sell them at remunerative prices? To imagine that is to accuse them of being stupid-and they are not stupid, or they would not be where they are. It would not be necessary to have the government take over the plant. All you have to do is to guarantee wages and prices, and put purchasing power into the hands of the people so that they may buy. Do that, and the trouble will clear up immediately.
And in six months they like to buy more-and it will start all over again.
If the hon. member will come to my office I will talk to him. Obviously I cannot conduct him through a full course in economics right here on the floor of the house. But if he will come to my office
I will.
-I will answer his questions so that he will not be able to say a word.
Is it a challenge?

In fact, I will offer him this challenge: If he will bring five of his friends who are not prejudiced one way or another and set them down in my office, I will undertake to answer every one of his questions so fully that his five friends will declare they are answered. There can be no question about it at all.
I take the challenge.

I am not afraid of it, because I have done it before.
Under the C.C.F., or under any socialistic technique through which we would have government ownership, where would a plant sell its goods? How would it sell those goods on the world markets? One can readily understand how it could sell its goods on the world markets if the government were prepared to use a social credit technique, that of subsidizing exports where necessary to sell exports abroad. I can understand that. Under that system I could see where they would sell their goods abroad. I believe the Ford Motor Company could do it, as a private organization. But may I hasten to say that social credit would not bother subsidizing goods to be sold abroad in competition with goods from factories within a given nation. That is, we would not undertake to force our goods into the world markets. If a nation wanted our goods, well and good. But if it were a matter of putting our goods into the hands of another nation to displace its industry, we would be against it. I thought it was necessary to say that, because some people might misunderstand.
I believe I have said enough at this time. Hon. members in this group are entirely in sympathy with the struggle being made by the Ford Motor Company employees. We realize they are doing things which they feel they would not like to do but which the government, because of the attitude it has taken, is forcing them to do. And the Ford plant is taking measures it is not justified in taking. Once more, by persisting in the present financial system, the government is forcing them into that position.
All I would say is simply this: Let the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), get permission from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), who seems to be the one who runs the whole show, to go to the Ford plant and say to them, Look here, gentlemen; this problem must be solved, and it must be solved right away. I am not going to suggest to him the measures he should take. But I will say that it can be done, and I will say further that it must be done, if Canada's economic and social structure is to be preserved. If the minister cannot solve it under the present system, then I urge upon him that with all possible speed he adopt a system under which he can solve it.
When I read the figures I have in my hand possibly some hon. members will wonder just to what extent they are in accordance with those supplied by the bureau of statistics. For those who wish to have the information authentically may I read this letter dated

Ford Motor Plant Strike
September 25,	1945, from the Dominion
Bureau of Statistics, and addressed to me in the following words:
Further to our telephone conversation1 of this morning regarding the percentage of wage-earners receiving various amounts of income.
The percentage of wage-earners earning less than $450 for the 12 months' period prior to the date of the census, June 2, 1941, was 32-9 per cent. 28-7 per cent of the wrage-earners reported earnings between $450 and $949; 29-9 per cent earned between $950 and $1,949 and 6-8 per cent earned $1,950 and over. 1-7 per cent of the wage-earners did not state the amount of earnings for the year.
For your information I am enclosing herewith census bulletins showing the earnings of wage-earners by occupation and the earnings and employment of wage-earners for the various census divisions or counties as well as a number of urban centres in Canada. The above statistics are taken from these bulletins.
Yours very truly,
J. L. Forsyth,
Statistician.
So that hon. members may see these bulletins, I am holding them up in my hand. I think this will serve as a basis upon which to do our future thinking.
We shall have more discussion along these lines by and by.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: AGE AND INCOME REQUIREMENTS-PROPOSED INCREASE IN AMOUNTS PAYABLE

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, October 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Maclnnis:
That, in the opinion of this house, the time has arrived -when consideration should be given to amending the Old Age Pension Act by lowering the pensionable age to sixty years, by increasing the amount of the pension so as to enable the recipients to live in health and selfrespect, and by deleting the income requirements for eligibility.

subtopic: AGE AND INCOME REQUIREMENTS-PROPOSED INCREASE IN AMOUNTS PAYABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to-night to speak to this resolution, but my colleague who was to resume the debate to-night has been unavoidably detained and so I am going to say a few words in support of the resolution pending his arrival.
The resolution speaks for itself. The time has come when in the interests not only of humanity but of our whole economic structure the old age pension should be raised so that people who have approached the eventide

of life may be able to live in comfort and decency. I do not think anyone in this house will contend to-day that an old age pension of $30 a month even at the age of seventy is sufficient in the kind of economy in which we are living. From time to time figures are produced by the bureau of statistics to show that more than twice that amount is required to meet the bare necessities of living in this country; and to expect our people to live at a rate of $30 a month or $1 a day is, I think, altogether wrong at this time. We have just concluded a great war, and our industrial equipment is now many times as large as it was before the war. We are now engaged in reconverting war industry to peace-time needs. Hence it is right not only to maintain but to extend the purchasing power of the people in order that they may buy the goods which can be manufactured with our largely improved machinery and skills.
This afternoon we were discussing, for example, the rates of wages that should be paid in industry. One could discuss in the same vein the prices which must be paid for agricultural products in order that the producer might have his purchasing power largely increased. And now here in the old age pensioners we have a group of citizens getting on in years who should be retiring at sixty and enjoying the rest of their days, but who are now at seventy kept at a level far below that of a decent subsistence. Hence we believe that every consideration should be given by the government to this resolution.
There should be no means test. The means test can be readily eliminated, and if the pension is paid to all those who attain a certain age, then through our income tax structure the amount in excess of what is needed to maintain the standard of living to which the individual has been more or less used can be withdrawn by taxation as not being required to maintain the standards to which I have referred.
We therefore believe that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) in moving this resolution has placed before the house something which deserves the support of every member on all sides of this chamber. I do not intend to say more except that I am, of course, in thorough accord with the resolution, which I hope will be recommended to the government for its consideration and early action.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I proceed with my remarks on the resolution, I wish first of all to compliment you, as I did when you received your appointment, upon your elevation to the

Old Age Pensions
Speakership of the House of Commons. In extending my congratulations to you in my letter I stated that I fully realized you were thoroughly qualified to hold the position. Also I told you that I was hoping that I might get the position myself. This was an absolutely legitimate hope, I think in view of my experience as Deputy Speaker and as one of the old-time members of the House of Commons. I am now, I believe, the senior Liberal member for the province of Ontario, and, like you, I myself have come up the hard way fighting every inch of the way to make my mark in the section of Ontario where I went as a pioneer nearly forty-five years ago. It was a hard thing to see the prize escape my grasp. However, we must take these things in our stride. I know that the position of Speaker is in absolutely capable and responsible hands, and I am sure that you will enjoy the cooperation of every section of the House of Commons, just as I did in the two years that I was Deputy Speaker of the house.
I should like to take this first opportunity I have had of speaking to this body and thanking every member of the House of Commons from 1943 to the last general election for the wonderful cooperation that I received from every hon. member.
It is not necessary for me to say that I am in agreement with the resolution which has been brought forward by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). It must strike particularly the new members of parliament when they see what we call private members' day function in this House of Commons. It is practically the only opportunity open to every private member during the session to give expression to his sentiments and to bring forcefully before the house the matters in which he and his constituents are interested. I vividly recollect when I was first elected member of the House of Commons. I sat in the farther corner of the house and for three or four days I listened to the debate on the speech from the throne and was puzzling why there was so much deliberation. At first it seemed futile. But after a few days it dawned upon me that I was hearing the voice of the maritimes, the voice of central Canada, Quebec and Ontario, the voice of the prairie provinces and of British Columbia. Here I heard discussed all the problems of every part of Canada, and I should like to say to the premiers of the different provinces in the Canadian confederation: Do not worry too much over provincial prerogatives and initiative because every federal member of the House of Commons is primarily a muni-cipalist, then a provincialist, and then a
federalist. So that there are all the necessary safeguards so far as provincial government activities and autonomy are concerned.
No one has ever doubted the sincerity of the mover of the resolution now before us. I for one during my first years of association with the hon. member for Vancouver East in parliament and in committees was inclined to be a little impatient with him. Of course, I shall never be a socialist. But after I had had an opportunity of sitting with the hon. member for Vancouver East and listening to him from time to time I was convinced of his sincerity of purpose, just as I was when he made his presentation the other day in moving this resolution.
If the Chair wanted to rigidly follow the rules of the house the resolution might have been held to be out of order, because the subject of old age pensions is on the agenda of the next dominion-provincial conference. However, I believe it was a fine thing to allow the discussion of old age pensions by every section of the house. The hon. member, in speaking of finance, said he did not know very much about it, and I believe he remarked that he was not well informed on problems of money. But he said also, in the statistics he gave the house, that to implement the scheme contemplated in his resolution would mean the expenditure of $800 million. That is interesting, for the party to which he belongs is definitely opposed to either inflation or deflation. They will never allow anything which in their opinion would inflate or deflate the earnings of the workers and farmers of this country. When I make that statement I have in mind a resolution which I believe was brought forward a year or two ago by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), who was worrying about what would happen to the bonds belonging to the Canadian people, fearing that they might lose some of their value. We had a good discussion. I know that as far as the house was concerned there was no demagogy about it.
But I could go farther on the same lines if I wanted to. To this resolution I could present an amendment asking, for instance, that old age pensions be paid to people at fifty or fifty-five years of age, and that they should receive S75 or 8100 a month. But we must remain within the limits of realism. After all, here we are in the federal forum looking after the affairs of this country, and this should be done in a national way. I believe that without exception every hon. member is progressive-minded. We fully realize that the days of the common man have

been ushered in, and that there will be no retreat. The New Deal spirit must carry on. It is absolutely impossible to reverse our direction, and nobody would want it. At the same time in our -discussions we must keep away from demagogy, for eventually the people will analyse and pass judgment upon our actions.
As I have said, it would be easy for me this evening to go much farther than the hon. member for Vancouver East, but I do not belive it would be fair to my constituents, to parliament, or to the country. Let me refer to one statement he made which I do not fully understand. In quoting statistics of persons of certain age groups he said that there were 610,000 employed, the remainder being nearly 700,000, and he created the impression that these latter were unemployed. I well remember a few years ago that an hon. member, when speaking or a matter of that kind, made the statement, relating to one phase of modern life, that every farmer should have at least two wives. As far as I was concerned as a single man, I was highly scandalized, but when I came to analyse his statement I thought there was some realism about it. In any event, to my mind the hon. member for Vancouver East created the impression that nearly 700,000 of these people were unemployed. It occurs to me that probably these people, or most of them, were unemployable. They may have been housewives or engaged in some similar occupation. Therefore the statistics he gave did not entirely convince me. When we discuss matters of this kind we must see the whole picture; we must survey the entire social programme of parliament; otherwise our judgments may be unfair. It is very easy, for instance, to single out and emphasize one item. Take health insurance: the implementing of that reform must be considered in relation to other reforms; you cannot single out one and leave the others out of account. Therefore I say that I have been pleased at the nature of the deliberation which has taken place so far upon this matter. We cannot afford to be backward; we are now going forward. I was greatly pleased at the fine cooperation which was shown last summer at the dominion-provincial conference between the federal administration and the premiers of the nine provinces. There were no "poor relations" there; we were all Canadians; all seemed to be equal. I hope as an Ontarian that the premier of the banner province will find it possible to maintain the same constructive attitude all the way through. The same should apply to Quebec and British Columbia, and,

indeed, to all the provinces. They are in the same position as far as this country nationally is concerned as Canada is in the international sphere. If people are suffering in Europe, if there is a depressed Asia, one feels no sense of security. The same applies to Canada; if some sections of this country are prosperous while others are depressed we shall not have unity and prosperity. I must give the highest praise to the premier of every province for the fine spirit of cooperation which was shown last summer when they met in Ottawa to discuss dominion-provincial questions. I hope most sincerely that that spirit will be maintained one hundred per cent. We come from different provinces, but there is one great unifying power, which is Canada, our only country.
I wish to touch briefly on pensions and insurance, and I should like the house to make a clear distinction between the two. As far as I am concerned I shall always be in favour of pensions for the blind, the invalids, the infirm, and the veterans. On the other hand there are those who in my opinion are not entitled to pensions. During the last election I told the people of my constituency that I was in favour of a scheme of old age insurance whereby a person who reached the age of nineteen or twenty-one should pay a nominal sum per month-for example, eight or ten or twelve cents-and that he would receive at the age of sixty or sixty-five the sum of $50 a month. I believe that is the best approach as far as old age pension is concerned. I do not believe in hand-outs to people who are able to look after themselves. Under the present system I have seen many injustices. How glad I was when I heard that under the new scheme, which I believe will be accepted by all the provinces, because it will be paid for out of the federal treasury, the sum of $30 a month will be paid without a means test. That, in my opinion, is a step in the right direction. I have never favoured the means test, because I believe it created many injustices to people who had a small nest-egg.
It is often contended at the present time that the government should be the mother and father and protector of the Canadian people. I still believe in individualism. I still think people should try to work for themselves. I repeat that for the moment there is no better scheme than the old age pension, but I hope the day is not far distant when there will be inaugurated a fine scheme of old age insurance. The thing is possible. We

Old Age Pensions
are going to adopt health insurance, and I know of no person in Canada who expects to receive health benefits without paying a certain amount for them.
After all, the government cannot accomplish miracles. I should not like to be in the position of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) at the present time. He is in a different position from that of the hon. member for Vancouver East, who in speaking on his resolution said he was not worried because the cost of old age pensions under his scheme would be $800 million. While sitting as chairman of a committee of the house, I tabulated the requests made one evening on the different government departments, and they made a total of $2,300 million-in one night alone! It is easy to make demands on governments, but one must cut his sail according to his cloth. We all sympathize with the Minister of Finance, for we know that, although he would like to implement all the logical requests which are made to the treasury, it is absolutely impossible for him to do so.
I do not believe in decrying my own country, nor do I think it behooves any member of parliament to speak in large terms of other countries and to suggest that they are better off than we are. We shall always have problems to solve but they can be solved and we should not be ashamed of our country. Far from it, we should be proud of our achievements not only during the war but in peace time. We must look forward, and our actions should be guided in one direction, namely, to work for the common man, to see that no one suffers and that everyone is given a chance to make a full, prosperous and comfortable living.
We have been forward-looking in all our legislation. Take the old province of Ontario, for example. In this province we have the mothers' allowance, which was a progressive piece of legislation, whereby a maximum of $80 a month has been paid to widowed mothers; and now we have family allowances. No one will say that this legislation is beyond criticism. I will not say to-night that the family allowance provisions are absolutely perfect, but the measure, has certainly been a marvellous thing for our people. I can assure you, sir, that many people in my section of the country, farmers, settlers who have worked hard all summer trying to put in a crop under difficult climatic conditions, have found the family allowance a blessing. It will enable them to remain the year round on their farms, so that they can look after their stock. I believe it has been a blessing.
I have made a special study of the manner in which the family allowance has been handled and the distribution of the money, and I can say that out of 100 cases I do not know of a single instance in which the parents, mother or father, will fail to husband every last dollar of that money. And for what purpose? To provide better food and clothing and in many cases better education for their children. On that score alone, I believe that this parliament, which was unanimous in the passing of that great social reform, should be complimented.
I repeat, a great deal of credit should be given the hon. member for Vancouver East for introducing this resolution, and those hon. members who have spoken on the subject also deserve our congratulations. At the same time, we must remain realistic. When I say that, I have in mind what has taken place in other countries, and let me say here that I do not intend to digress into a discussion of the political situation anywhere else. But during the election in Great Britain I received the London Times and there I read that the parties in opposition were making great promises. I am not worrying, of course, but I know the promises then made by one party in opposition, to-day the Socialist government, will not be implemented. They will not be able to carry out all the things they promised the British people. Only a few days ago they intimated that the coal situation will be no better than it was a year ago.
In other words, the moment you are harnessed with the responsibility of government you find what a sobering effect that responsibility has. I have been told by some gentlemen, married friends of mine, that before they got married they made fine promises to their brides-to-be. They were going to provide a grand piano, a. fine house, a fine car, and so on. But the moment they got married they discovered that it could not be done because they had not the means. The same applies to . governments. Governments would like to comply with the various requests that are made of them, but that is absolutely impossible.
Even to-day, now that we have peace, we shall have a budget of $4 billion, which will be raised in this way: $2,500 million by way of taxation and $1,500 million through borrowing. No matter what we say about gearing our financial structure to take care of our peace requirements as we did for war purposes, it will not be possible. However, I have never taken a disproportionate view of the so-called depression and I am puzzled sometimes by the socialist party when they bring up that topic. They had no infallible

Old Age Pensions

remedy for the depression from 1930 to 1939. They had no formula by which to bring about better conditions. The then Prime Minister of Canada may have made mistakes, but he tried to do his best. But what was the spectacle we saw in the great republic to the south of us? Could they solve the depression there? Could the people in Europe solve the depression over there? No, because all the great nations were caught in it. However, we have learned some lessons, and for my part I will never tolerate a depression of the same depth and breadth as that which we had twelve years ago. I do not think it is fair for the socialist party on every single occasion to talk about the depression. One would think it was their wish that we should have another depression. Experience has shown, and the progressiveness of parliament gives us some reassurance in this regard, that we shall never have another depression such as we had before. It is unthinkable that we should have had a bath of blood, so to speak, slaughter for the last six years throughout the world, only to end in that way.
Personally, I think it is my duty as a member of parliament to go to my people and tell them to sacrifice in a matter of meat rationing, to make other sacrifices, short of bloodshed, comparable with those which they made during the war, so that we may be able to solve the problems of peace. But I will not make any appeal to their passions.
This afternoon I listened attentively to the debate and I thought it was on a high level. No one can doubt the sincerity of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) *when he speaks on labour matters. At the same time I believe that every other member of parliament has at heart as much as he has, the welfare of our workers and of our farmers as well. The same remarks apply to the question now before the house.
Before concluding, may I express the hope that when the premiers of the different prov- [DOT] inces come here again they will be imbued with the same spirit of unity, the same spirit of Canadianism that animated them this summer. Old age pensions must be discussed again and the legislation perhaps amended. Perhaps the monthly payment should be higher. At the same time we must be practical and logical. I fervently hope that health insurance will be implemented in every section of Canada because we are all united on that question. I hope also that the deputations, every time they speak, will think of the country as a whole and not of their own individual interests.

If they do, it will be all the easier for me to inspire my own people. I could go to the people in the lumbering section of my constituency and say, "You do not have enough butter or sufficient sugar or meat", but it is not my duty to do so and I do not believe that other hon. members wish to do that.
I hope that Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, the provinces which are supposed to be more privileged than the others by reason of geographical, industrial and financial considerations, will think of the country as a whole and not merely of their own particular localities. Although I am a Liberal I wish to pay tribute to Mr. George Drew, Premier of Ontario, for the fine spirit he showed at the conference, and also to Mr. Duplessis. I am not talking politics; I am speaking as a Canadian, and he realized that the whole is greater than any of its parts. He realized that we must work in unison if we are to reach our goal of nationhood and prosperity and comfort for every citizen of Canada.

I say at the outset that I have a feeling of much sadness for my hon. friend (Mr. Bradette) who has just concluded such a fine speech. I had not known until to-night that it was anything more than just ordinary bad luck that had caused him to remain single. I now understand from what he has said that the real fact is that he did not get married because of his own intellectual honesty; he could not bring himself to make those vast pre-marital promises which resulted in success for nearly all of the hon. members of this house. I should like to say to him that even yet he may succeed, and he need not be concerned about such promises, because, as every married man comes to find out, he does not really become successful by those lies that he tells. He finds out, after somewhere between two, ten or maybe fifteen years, that he was not believed anyway. Underneath her breath the lady is probably always saying, you are lying, I know, but it is pleasant. No real attention is paid to the lies; therefore, if the hon. gentleman still desires to get married he can just let himself go and make any promise he likes; it will not be held against him at all.
In speaking on this subject, Mr. Speaker, for just a few minutes may I say that there are two or three remarks which have been made in the course of this debate and in similar debates to which I should like to address myself. People say, what we can

Old Age Pensions
do in wartime, we can do in peace time. That is unquestionably true. I could never understand why there had to be so much emphasis put upon that statement as though there were some chance of argument in it, as though it were not self-evident. It seems to me it is self-evident that what you can do in war time you can do in peace time. It does, however, require certain conditions to be the same; it requires a psychological condition to be the same as in war time; it requires the very general agreement in the country that you have under the urge of patriotism.
One then has to examine just how it is that certain things have been done in war time, and just what will be necessary to be done in peace time in order to carry on in substantially the same way, that is, in the way of raising and spending money. If we disregard, for example, the method of producing money by printing it or by some other such means and decide that we are talking about the raising of money for the payment of social services in the same way we have hitherto done, then all that is necessary in order to pay the bill which is asked for in the resolution is to continue the same level of taxation that we have now, the same regimentation that we have now, and all that sort of thing.
Substantially what happened in 1939 and the years afterwards is something like this. In 1939 the Minister of Finance, speaking for the Canadian people, said, We will arrange that all people in the country who are working will work a little less for themselves, out of every hour's earnings a certain part will be used for the purpose of being handed to the Minister of Defence and the Minister of Munitions; they will take it and give it to other people who will do certain things to earn it. I recall that the first sum of money about which the Minister of Finance talked in that way was $100 million. It was not very long before it was also arranged that in addition to any contribution made by the people of Canada in that manner they would dig under their mattresses and would find money, purchasing power as it is sometimes called, and they would hand that over to the Minister of Finance in order that he might, in turn, pass it on to the other spending ministers, to be used by them in the manner that I have indicated. It was not very long after that before the Minister of Finance, in the name of the Canadian people, made a similar request, the only difference being that the second or third time he spoke he was not talking about any dribs and drabs and jots and tittles like $100 million; he went far beyond that. By this time it was not the case that a person had to
work about one-twenty-fifth of his time for the purpose of supplying spending money to * the Minister of Munitions and the defence ministers; it had reached the point in the case of the wealthy people where the contribution was half-time at least, and in the case of the less wealthy a somewhat lower proportion, but in the case of all a very considerable percentage of their time was to be devoted to raising the wherewithal for the spending ministers of the government to spend in the name of the Canadian people.
Substantially that is the way the money has been obtained. There is no question about that. There is no magic about it. It just meant that kind of hard work for all of the Canadian people; therefore, it is absolutely correct to say that what has been done in war time can be done in peace time, granted the will to do it. But you must have among the Canadian people an equal willingness to do this that you had under the urge of patriotism in war.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat spoke two or three times about the need of being realistic. Surely, Mr. Speaker, if we ask ourselves whether the Canadian people, any section of them, will be willing to continue to work that amount of time for the purpose of supplying spending money to the ministers of this government who will be charged with the distribution of such moneys as are dealt with in this resolution, we are bound to come to a negative answer. All across the country and in all classes of society at the present time there is a demand for the lowering of taxation. I do not know what the Minister of Finance is going to do on Friday, but it is perfectly certain we can say now, that large sections of the public will not be satisfied with the reductions in taxation which he will make. That dissatisfaction we shall find in the farming community; we shall find it in the section of the public which is made up of what we commonly call the white-collar workers; we shall find it among those to whom we sometimes refer as manual workers; we shall find it among those who are well to do, and we shall find it in the wealthy classes. There is no doubt in the world that the public of Canada will not continue to pay the taxation that they have been paying.
Such being the case, is it being realistic; is it cutting the coat according to the cloth when demands amounting to something between $700,000,000 and $850,000,000 are made in a resolution of this kind? I do not know the right figure; sometimes I have heard $700,000,000 and sometimes $850,000,000, but when one gets into figures as nearly astro-
Old Age Pensions

nomical as those probably it does not make any difference. In order to demonstrate that people will not continue to pay these taxes, no matter if the taxes are imposed, it is only necessary to look at what has already happened. Many men will not go to work on Saturday mornings because it does not pay them. Plenty of my friends have toldl me they do not see any sense in going to work on Saturday morning because they get such a very small amount of money for it. I have known men in the professional class who have refused certain commissions which were brought to them because their fee would be hardly worth while, since they were in an income bracket in which too large a percentage went, as they would say, to Mr. Ilsley. That sort of thing, to defeat taxation, grows apace once it gets started; and if people will do that, certainly they will much more easily defeat the loans which will be necessary for some time in order to carry on the business of the country. Apparently we have made up our minds that we shall carry on what is called deficit financing for a certain length of time; I do not know how long. We shall be raising considerable sums of money by taxation and endeavouring to raise further considerable sums by loans. Well, if people will not continue to pay taxes, much more strongly can it be asserted that they will not contribute to loans to keep up expenditures unless these expenditures are favourably viewed by one hundred per cent of the people, and there is nothing like that unanimity behind a proposition such as this. In the prosecution of a war which we could all say was indeed a war for liberty and, as the Prime Minister so frequently remarked, a crusade of righteousness, you could get unanimity, but that is not the case with a social measure of this kind. To go farther than the people of the country would desire at any given time is only to endanger other things.

speechtext:
Unfortunately I did not get all the question, but I think I have the sense of it. I believe my hon. friend asked if I was of opinion that any considerable number of people would oppose giving a larger pension and giving it to people at the age of sixty without any means test, as set forth in the resolution. Oh, yes, I am very strongly of that opinion. I have had many letters from people saying, "I am sixty years of age, Maybank, and by gad I don't need any pension; I don't think it is necessary yet." I 
have had that told me by a good many people, and I have had a great number of people write and say that unless taxes were reduced there just would not be any government in this country at all. I wonder that some of the writers who are penning these letters to me do not burn the paper with their words. I could not think of reading their letters in this house, because I am quite sure I should be ruled out for using blasphemous language. That is my opinion, at any rate; of course if I am wrong about that there is a way of finding out.
My remarks come down to this. At the present time I do not think this is a feasible proposition in the light of the present taxation; in the light of the attitude of most of the people in reference to taxation; in the light of the fact that a large social welfare programme is already envisaged which will involve the expenditure of a large sum of money, and in view of the fact that this proposal is non-contributor}'. That last remark leads me to say this. I am very much in favour of any kind of scheme that will be contributory. There are some features of the proposals which have been brought before the dominion-provincial conference which I do not like. The outstanding improvement that has been suggested is the payment to everybody afte^r the age of seventy, although I think that age is too great, and the payment of the pension from sixty-five to seventy years on somewhat the present basis. The matter of divided responsibility is a feature I do not like, but I feel that no person can deny that the present proposal of the government is an improvement over the existing practice. At the same time I do not like it as well >as I would like some plan purely contributory in nature, something to which my honourable friend who preceded me referred as insurance. It seems to me that old age pension payments constitute the type of social law that lends itself particularly and peculiarly to the insurance principle. I think it would be very much better, even at the present stage of the dominion-provincial conference, if everything could be dropped in favour of a straight insurance proposition. I know there are difficulties in the way. I know, for example, that already some people are under insurance schemes, such as civil servants and people who work on railroads and in a large number of industries. Even so, I believe it would be better to treat this particular branch of our social welfare legislation in a different way and put it under a straight insurance principle, make it an insurance scheme.
Some years ago I read in the Labour Gazette that at that time four per cent of our

Old Age Pensions
people were over seventy years of age, and of those four per cent, fifty per cent received the old age pension, which was $240 a year at that time. Just playing with the idea of insurance, I made some mental calculations. Upon the presumption, which would not hold good at all times, that money wouild yield five per cent interest, I soon realized that the payment of $1 by a' child the minute after it was born, if that could be done, would actually provide for its old age pension. I will tell honourable members how it worked out. At five per cent, in fourteen years that $1 would become $2. In another fourteen years it would become $4. By the time that child reached the age of seventy the $1 would become $32. From what I already said we see that one hundred people would pay into the fund. That is $3,200. Of that number, two people would draw pension, and a fund of $1,600 is more than enough for the average old age pension of $240 after the age of seventy.
I mention that only to illustrate what can be done. I do not claim complete accuracy in that example, but I mention it for this reason. It shows what can be done under a contributory scheme, as against this other type of old age pension.
Hon. members from the other side of the house have said that what I am really doing is simply taking up time, and their suggestion is that I am talking the case out. I wish to deny as sharply and as emphatically as I can any such allegation. Those hon. members who speak in that way remind me very much of an old deaf and dumb gentleman who was a cooper, and whom I knew at one time. This gentleman used to have arguments and, as mutes must, he expressed himself with his fingers. After he had spoken, if I may use that word, he turned his head away which was the only way he could prevent anyone else from saying anything. He feared an answer.

Some have spoken in opposition to the means test. In my opinion it has always been objectionable. I had a good deal to do with it in those days when, because of the circumstances of the post I held, I was forced to administer relief. It is just about as disheartening an experience as anyone can have thrust upon him. Yet we have to admit that in every country where there is an old age pension system, and where it is not contributory, there is a means test.
Again, being realistic, I do not believe it will ever for long be wiped out, while old age pensions are paid out of general taxation. This is another reason, in my opinion, for old age pensions being placed on an insurance principle, and not coming out of general taxation, because, depend upon it, whether you like it or not the time will come, every once in a while, when either the means test will be placed upon people who are receiving from taxation, or the circumstances of payment will be changed, or something of that sort will be done.
I suppose it would be right to say that any such remark as that is made in sadness. But that is the truth of the matter, and those are the facts of human nature. Just as long as pensions are paid out of taxation there will be problems of that sort. And the only way to have pensions paid is, as a matter of right, resulting from insurance. As a matter of fact, the means test in this country is more severe than it is in New Zealand; at least I would think so, from my reading of the law. I realize, of course, that one can never tell for certain, until he actually gets down to administration. But those hon. members who extol New Zealand-it being the most distant country in the world1, and therefore the greenest-should remember that down there they first exact an insurance premium from the citizen, and following that they give him the means test. They do both.
But we never hear hon. members say that. First of all, in New Zealand they exact a certain sum of money by way of insurance, part of which goes to old age pensions; and then they pay the old age pension only according to the means test. It is a somewhat more generous means test than the one in this country, but at least it does not come anywhere near giving a free pension to all.

Everybody knows that. But, mind you, Mr. Speaker, that must not be taken as final and definite. Evidently the hon. member thinks that from the wording of the resolution a contributory system could be meant. Well, if that is what is meant, then of course I can only say that the mover of the resolution and those various persons who have spoken 100 per cent in favour of it might have been a little more clear. If they had, it would have put the debate on an entirely different plane. Of course there would not be any means test if you were first paying for it. The reference in the resolution to relinquishing means test is in the words which seem to me to preclude any idea of contribution. It would not have occurred to me-perhaps I am just a little dumb-that a person would propound a resolution which would be condemnatory of the means test when, all the time, he had in his mind that a contribution not referred to in the resolution would first be exacted from the beneficiary of the scheme.
I have given the hon. member that much explanation of the reason why I have spoken as though there were to be no contribution. However, that is about as far as I can go at the present time, because I see my time has expired.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not very often that I rise in the house to take part in a labour dispute. I represent, as most hon. members know, an agricultural constituency. But I believe that this particular strike is of vital importance not only to the locality in which it is taking place but to the whole of our Canadian economy.
The strikers at Windsor, as has been said to-day, are coming out fighting for a certain principle, and that principle is that their take-home pay shall not be reduced during the period following this war. The farmers in my part of the country regard this strike as their first line of defence. They are vitally interested in seeing that the take-home pay of the workers in the Ford plant is maintained because they have had a demonstration in this war of what it means to agriculture to have spending power in the hands of the workers of Canada, and any attempt by this government or by private enterprise in Canada to reduce the wages of the worker would have a repercussion on agriculture generally throughout the country. Agriculture recognizes that if the take-home pay of the worker is reduced, it will mean within one year less money for what agriculture has to sell. The farmers will sell . less butter, less eggs, less milk, less fruit, and less of all those other farm products which the worker buys. So that agricuture is vitally interested in seeing that the standards of living in Canada are maintained.
Ford Motor Plant Strike

Certain people speaking in agricultural communities have tried to create an entirely wrong impression in the farmer's mind with respect to the pay the worker in industry actually receives. Only to-day in the house certain hon. members wanted to know what these automobile workers received per hour. I have heard speakers in country districts say: Yes, workers in the automobile industry receive SI an hour. Immediately the impression is created in the farmer's mind who works fourteen hours a day: That means $14 a day. The farmer works thirty days in the month, for he has to milk his cows and feed his stock every day, so that he figures that the automobile worker receives thirty times $14, or $420 a month, or about $5,000 a year, and naturally he thinks these fellows are getting fairly well paid. But that is not what happened. Statistics show that the average take-home pay of the workers in the automotive industry before the war was a little better than $1,200 a year. They want to advance that by thirty per cent to have take-home pay of approximately $1,800 a year. Every farmer in Canada realizes that $1,800 a year is not an excessive salary, that it will do no more than permit the average working man to have a reasonable standard of living. Therefore I tell the government that I believe agriculture in this country is behind the workers at this time in their efforts to maintain the rates of pay which they have been receiving during the war, and I think the government will find that out before this is over.
Another point. It is the government that are paying for this strike. If I understand correctly, the Ford Motor Company of Canada have made sufficient profits this year; any further profits would go into the excess profits tax, and the government get over ninety per cent of those additional profits, so that the company are not interested in whether the plant opens or not. But I say that the government should be interested because they are paying for this strike; they are the people who are actually maintaining the Ford Motor Company's position in keeping these people locked out of the plant. The people of Canada, not the Ford Motor Company, are paying for it. I bring that point to the attention of the minister and to the government, so that the people in the country will know what the position is.
I believe that other hon. members representing agricultural districts should rise and express their opinions and what they believe to be the opinions of the people they represent with respect to these strikes. It is a serious situation which we are facing in Canada. It is
[Mr. Wright.1
a serious situation which we are facing on the North American continent. We in this house cannot afford to remain quiet about it.
