I rise at this time as a farmer member to add my voice to what our group, including the hon. member who has just taken his seat, has said on this subject. It is our group, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group, which has tried to bring before the people the important fact that to-day Canadians are interdependent. To-day they have come to realize that it makes no difference whether you are a worker in industry or a farmer, you are entitled to a decent standard of living. I rise to-day recognizing this truth, that if we are to win the peace we must win this fundamental fight to establish a minimum wage scale in industry.
As a practical farmer I say that farmers recognize that the Canadian industrial worker is our best customer, and we are interested in seeing that he gets a decent wage. Now that the nations of the world- have gathered, as they did at Hot Springs, Virginia, and recognized the duty of setting a minimum standard for the world, we as Canadian people have a first and domestic responsibility of establishing that standard for our own people. The leader of our group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) asked earlier in the session that $25 a week be set as a floor for wages. That is a very good beginning, but we realize that we must have a wage scale in harmony with the cost of living, and similar treatment in respect of the things which agriculture produces. This is a fight in which all members of the house have -to take part. The good things which we can produce in Canada should be made available to the Canadian people. In the past the enemies of the common people, in the form of established big business, tried to divide and rule. To-day we must recognize as a Christian nation the dignity of labour and the right of the people who work to have decent -homes and decent conditions of employment.
In conclusion, I will say only this, that two things are necessary, namely, the establishment of unions and the provision of security. As a practical farmer I say that we recognize at this time the need for action on the part of this government.

What happened in that country? May I say to my good Conservative friends that business went to

the state, trade unions went to the state, insurance went to the state, banks went to the state; and when Hitler came along these people thought they were free individuals, whereas actually they were servants of the state. And what happened? It is a matter of history that when he got his fingers on the ammunition he said, "This is the way you are going or else", and within twenty-four hours there was a dictatorship supplanting democracy in Germany and no trade unions. To use the simple language of the man in the street, any fool can govern the country with a bayonet in his hand as long as he does not stick it into himself. That is simple.

speechtext: I am taking the implication. My hon. friend the member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) says, "Who said so?" That is what good solid German socialists all said, "Who said so?" maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext: I saw that, too. I was in Germany when the revolution happened and that is why I am so sincere about this. Therefore I say this to my hon. friends. If, my hon. friends, were in power for one session, the reflection of their attitude toward the nation would be in the opposite direction the same as it was in Germany, where you had the development of a powerful communist party which reflected itself in the Hitler movement.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext: You are not mixing us up with the communist party, surely?

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-STRIKE AT FORD MOTOR PLANT, WINDSOR
speechtext: I am talking about the swing of the pendulum. My hon. friends are so clever that they do not see much farther than the next election. What I am pointing out to my hon. friends is this. Things move along from one stage to another until freedom has disappeared-freedom as we understand it.

Ford Motor Plant Strike
I am going to go briefly over the steps that led to this dispute, and I speak quite sincerely and without bias toward one side or the other. I do not think all the faults are on one side. I do not believe that in any dispute, whether family, industrial or business dispute, the faults are all on one side. One hon. member in the opposition said today that this dispute had been in existence for seventeen months-
Right.

-that it had been pushed around for seventeen months. That is hardly fair. We have used the best negotiators and conciliators there are in this dominion to compose the dispute. The basic policy of the government made possible the organization of the men who work in the Ford plant and Chrysler and General Motors at Oshawa and Windsor. We went through all the machinery that was established, machinery that has been approved by the trades union organizations of this country, machinery that is administered equally bv the workers and the employers in industry, with a judge or minister of labour as chairman of the respective boards. We sent Mr. Justice Richards, I think it is fair to say, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Justice Richards is one of the ablest conciliators in the dominion. We sent him into the dispute in Windsor; he was unsuccessful.
A board of conciliation was established within twenty-four hours under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice O'Connor, another able conciliator from Edmonton, in an effort to pull the dispute out of the fire. What was the finding of that board? The majority finding was for a check-off, a limited checkoff, it is true. They discarded the closed shop idea. I think, if my memory serves me correctly, Mr. Speaker, even the representative of the employees did not approve the arguments put forward in that dispute for the closed shop. I think that representative's name was Bora Laskin.
These are the words of Mr. Justice O'Connor, the chairman of the board:
We are none of us prepared to recommend a provision for a union shop but the chairman and Mr. Laskin are prepared to recommend that the parties agree to a voluntary check-off irrevocable during the term of the contract as a solution of the present difficulty.
May I go a step farther and say this also. This is a tribute paid by the chairman of that board to the departments of labour in the dominion and in the province of Ontario:

Let nothing be done or said that will interfere with the effort to solve this particular dispute. Let the management realize its responsibility. Let it realize that by taking the union into its confidence, in the pursuit of what the Minister of Labour mentioned to-night, the industrial council idea and the democratization of industry, no one will lose by that kind of trust.
These parties, for reasons which I know, but which I think I should not mention at this stage, have engendered suspicion and hate which is not shared alone by the men working in that plant. That must go. It must disappear, and a basis of mutual confidence and good faith in one another must be restored in that plant and in others so that they can get down to work on a democratic basis, not only in the interests of the company but in the interests of the men. I believe that in working for the interests of the men the interests of all are involved.
We are faced with a situation wherein we are trying to reconcile a difficult dispute. The discussion to-day reveals that on all sides of the house, no particular group has any monopoly of interest in the welfare of the workers or in the interests of settling this dispute. There is a common recognition that good faith must be restored between the parties and that at the earliest moment steps must be taken consistent with our ability to effect a final solution between the parties involved.
Knowing the difficulties, and particularly in the light of my experience over this very week-end, I believe that objective is being approached as well as, under the circumstances and having in mind the interests of everyone, that can be done. This discussion has served one purpose, namely, to bring the matter into bold relief. It has served to confirm once again, through the Minister of 47696-56
Labour, the merit of trade union organization and the desirability of the management understanding this and realizing the dire consequences, otherwise, not only for' itself but for our country.
Perhaps this will not be the last discussion we shall have on matters like this, but I say to all groups in this house, no matter what our political parties may be, that there is an obligation, in the discussion of these matters, to give an example to those who find themselves involved in this dispute. It is in that frame of mind that I have entered into this discussion, and once again I affirm my belief in the right of trade union organization, and I urge the management to do everything it can to see that the purposes, the noble purposes, of the trade union effort are not needlessly disintegrated.

I had not intended originally to enter this debate. The house has devoted almost the whole day to speaking about my neighbours and my friends, and in fact speaking about many who were my comrades in the last five or six years, and I think it is just as well that the house should know that these men are neither dupes nor tools, nor are they stupid. For just a minute we can turn the eyes of reason rather than emotion in that direction.
I think the strike is an economic contest coolly planned and conducted as though it were a horse trade or a transaction on St. James street. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) said that the issue was the grievance procedure; the minister on the other hand says that the issue is union security. Odd as it may be, they are, I believe, both right. The negotiations actually broke down on grievance procedure. They might have broken down on anything if the parties did not have good will and wanted them to break down as they did in this case. Actually the union wanted union security. In so far as I am concerned, in so far as my own personal position is concerned, if it interests the house, they know very well where I stand, and I have stood there for a very long time. I am not only a believer but a supporter of union security. But what the house has lost sight of, I think-and this is no fault of the Department of Labour, because they have provided the machinery-is that for seventeen months the negotiations have been bedevilled by hearings and boards and lawyers and politicians, or would-be politicians, with the result that the animosities have now become the ruling factor and everybody has lost sight of the principle involved and of the poor people



Ways and Means-Interim Supply
who are now walking the streets. The animosities have become so deep, so bitter and so unrelenting between the company and the men that any conference table that will have any chance of success now must have new faces in new places.
The hon. member said that it was a matter of grievance procedure that upset the applecart; well, it might have been anything. I have lived with this problem longer than any other hon. member. I have lived with it for many years, and it has always been a struggle for these men. It has been a very long struggle and there have been many casualties, but they have all been on one side.
If we have done anything at all here today we have certainly indicated that we are not complacent about it; we certainly do not intend to sit it out. What we need at this particular time is to get at the root of the trouble and provide some leadership. The whole country is watching. What are we to do with the Ford strike? This will be a precedent; it will be the formula. *
I was gratified to hear the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) say that his approach was conciliation and peace. That is everyone's approach; but we must make sure that it does not get down to the point where it becomes a knock-'em-down and a drag-'em-out contest. Then it becomes too late. I do not think it is suggested from this side of the house or from any side of the house that we should dictate at this time to either one party or the other. But I do think that under P.C. 4020 the minister possesses authority to summon either Mr. Campbell or the union leaders.
Let the responsibility be with those who do not appear at the summons of the minister, and the people of this country will judge, and judge only too well. All that we can ask here to-day is that they be called togeth. i that they be put into a room. Let them decide; let them talk it out. Mr. Bevin, Mr. Molotov and Mr. Byrnes are having their troubles too. They are going back to try to talk it out to see what happens. These are not the only troubles in the world. We have to give them a chance.
It seems to me that the minister has been trying to do it. He is a better judge of what should be done than those of us who sit outside; but the danger is just this, and we must face up to it. If we do not give leadership at this particular time men who have different ideologies and men who have direct tactics may take over, in which case it may be too late. It is our duty in this

house to see that these instincts are channelled through democratic purposes; then we can feel safe.
I was gratified to sit in this house and to hear from all sides the kind of talk that would at least tell some industrialists in this country that if they have the bugler ready to blow taps on trade unionism they had better fire that bugler because trade unionism is here to stay. So far as I am concerned I cannot picture this country without a strong and responsible trade union movement. I can well remember; and the house can well remember, that in any fascist country the trade union movement fell first, and when we liberated the countries they rose first. They are the very core of democracy and we must preserve them.
I say again we are not asking the minister to take sides: it would not be fair at this time. But the minister has prerogatives. The minister can exercise his good office in order to get these people together for the purpose of talking out their problem. That problem can and must be talked out so that these people can get back to work again.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. C. ABBOTT (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a week ago when I had almost completed my opening statement with respect to the naval estimates I had just finished telling the committee that it was expected the main fleet bases on the east and west coasts would be maintained, but that most of the smaller bases would be closed. Continuing where I left, off, may I add that it is hoped to continue the naval division^, throughout the country. These establishments have been most valuable assets during the war and it is believed that they can prove their worth during peace.
Our establishments abroad are to be in large measure closed down. H.M.C.S. Niobe, the manning and training station near the Clyde in Scotland will be closed, probably before the end of the present fiscal year and 47696-56J
the property returned to its owners. The training base at Bermuda called Somers Isles is now being closed'. In Newfoundland, our facilities are being reduced to care and maintenance or are being closed as the need dictates.
During the war the Royal Canadian Navy maintained a division for operational research. Tlie principal members of this group were four physicists, two astrophysicists, and two mathematicians. The group was generally directed by Doctor J. H. L. Johnstone, O.B.E., and Doctor G. H. Henderson, O.B.E., both professors of physics at Dalhousie university. A close liaison was maintained with the national research council, and with the research organizations at the admiralty and in the United States navy. The section was not large but the work done was helpful. While it may be difficult to continue naval scientific research on an extensive scale during peace time, it will be generally agreed, I think, that the service should keep itself abreast of developments in the field and that an adequate organization and facilities for that purpose must be maintained.
I think perhaps I should now give the committee some precise figures on the operation of the convoy system, particularly in the north Atlantic during the war years. This was the theatre of war in which the Canadian navy played its greatest part. From 1939 until the end of May, 1945, the Canadian navy convoyed 25,859 ships eastward and 16,823 westward. The deadweight tonnage carried by these ships to the United Kingdom was 235,104,856. Of the more than forty-two thousand ships convoyed by the R.C.N., only 438 were sunk by enemy action. The greatest number of sinkings took place in 1942 when 149 merchant ships in the R.C.N. convoys were lost. In the years 1940 and 1941 ships to the number of seventy-five each year were lost. In 1943, 125 were lost. By 1944, the German U-boat threat had been mastered and the merchant ship losses in R.C.N. convoys in that year fell to the rather insignificant figure of seven.
In addition to these transatlantic convoys, the R.C.N. ran twenty-one sets of coastal convoys on our eastern seaboard in the gulf and River St. Lawrence, to Newfoundland and to some UJ3. ports. The total number of merchant ships thus protected in these coastal convoys was 18,898. That record of operations is one of which Canadians may well take pride.
A word now as to the future. While, as is the case in the other services, final determination as to just what our naval establishment should be in the post-war period cannot yet be
87b
Demobilization-Naval Services

made, and will be influenced to a large extent by the nature of our obligations under world or regional security arrangements, it is possible to state with some accuracy what our establishment will iprobably be.
During the war our naval role was primarily that of escort duty, carried out by lighter ships, few of which would be suitable for permanent peace-time operation, and in fact the role which it was contemplated we would play in the Pacific war was of a different character to that performed in the Atlantic and required the use of other types of ships.
It is now proposed that at the outset Canada's peace-time navy should comprise two cruisers, probably two light fleet carriers, ten to twelve destroyers, and the necessary ancillary craft, all of these of the latest and most modern type, while in reserve and for training purposes, we will continue to hold a certain number of frigates. Such an establishment will require a force of about 10,000 officers and men.
I have another announcement to make which should be of interest to the members of the naval forces who have served in the second world war. As the committee knows, there 'have been three varieties of stripes in the Canadian naval	service-the broad
straight stripes of the permanent force, the curly stripes of the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve, and the wavy stripes of the R.C.N.V.R.
It is now proposed that, in addition to the permanent force, there shall be a single reserve force known as the "Royal Canadian Navy Reserve". This force will comprise1 all reserves, including reserve air personnel as well as personnel of the university naval training divisions. A set of regulations will cover the reserve R.C.N. The uniform will be similar in all respects to that worn by the members of the permanent force, and for the time being, the total authorized strength of the reserve will be 18,000, exclusive of those on the retired list. In due course further announcements will be made with respect to its organization. It is unlikely, however, that it will be possible to complete this until demobilization has been further advanced.
I cannot conclude my remarks without making some reference to the Royal Canadian Sea Cadets. Many of these lads gradu-dated from the corps into the Royal Canadian Navy during the war. From reports which have been made by officers of various ships in which these ex-sea cadets served it is clear that the training they received while in the corps was of great advantage to them in carrying out their duties. There are today between fourteen and fifteen thousand sea
cadets and officers in the ninety-three corps distributed throughout Canada, and the naval service will continue to extend its full cooperation to the effort being made to keep the corps up to strength.
I am grateful to the Navy League of Canada for its sponsorship of the corps throughout the dominion, and as naval minister I take some satisfaction in the part the naval service itself has played in the training of sea cadets and in the encouragement of the development of the corps by naval officers across the country. This supervision and encouragement will be continued in peace time for it is not only expected that the Royal Canadian Navy continue in the future as it has in the past to obtain recruits from the corps, but we also realize that the training received by the boys in that corps helps to make them better Canadian citizens.
In the course of the debate a little over a week ago a number of speeches were made. I would refer particularly, however, to the helpful and constructive speech of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). He made some suggestions, and at this time I would refer to two of them in particular.
One suggestion was that the statement with respect to the three defence services should be made at the same time in order that the committee might have the over-all picture. The same suggestion has been made by other hon. members, and there is much to commend it.
So far as my own two departments are concerned I should like to have been able to accept the suggestion; however, it was not feasible at this session. As hon. members will realize, a large part of the estimates refate to past expenditures, and expenditures which carry over from the war period. I feel sure, however, that in future sessions that procedure should be followed, and I can see that it would be particularly helpful in considering the future-although not the past-of the three armed services.
I believe I could help to meet the wishes of the committee in this way. My colleague, the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Gibson) has given his statement, and I have now completed nfy statement with respect to the navy. Circumstances permitting, I would be ready to make a similar statement with respect to the army on Thursday, let us say, and the committee could then decide which set of detailed estimates it might wish to consider first.

Before the committee rises I should like to ask a question. At some point early in the discussion in committee will the Minister of National Defence give a break-down of expenditures under the following headings: War expenditures-these would include commitments of the past- demobilization expenditures, and what one might call expenditures for defence in the future. I should personally like to have such information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I should be very happy to do what I can to meet the wishes of the leader of the opposition on that point. As he probably knows, for the last four or five years our practice has been, in connection with these war estimates, to consider the estimates of the different services under twelve or thirteen primary headings such as civil salaries, pay and allowances, travel, transportation and freight and the like. The details have, in fact, been prepared on that basis.
I shall be ready to give any information or break-down that I can; but I am afraid that at this date it would be difficult, if not impossible, from a practical point of view completely to rearrange the estimates. However, I shall be happy to do what I can to break them down under the suggested headings. I must repeat, however, that I am
Demobilization-Naval Services

afraid it would be difficult to make a complete rearrangement of the way in which they are presented. I had more or less assumed that the committee would be ready to consider them in the form in which they were presented at the last three or four sessions. I realize, of course, that circumstances are somewhat different to-day, but they have become so quite recently, with the result that the accounting staffs have not been able to make any change in their method of presentation. I may say that these estimates I am going to bring before the house have already been revised three or four times since they were first prepared last March. Frankly I would hesitate to impose too great a burden upon our accounting staffs, which are already pretty heavily burdened. However, I shall try to meet my hon. friend in any way I can.

I was asking that the Minister of National Defence or indeed the minister of any other department revise the set-up of the estimates. I am not asking that at all. But I think the government, in its own interests, ought to let the house and the country know what proportion of these total expenditures amounting to $3,650 million would be chargeable to commitments with respect to the war; what proportion would be chargeable to demobilization and what proportion to the future defence plan for the three services. If that information cannot be given, then it cannot be given. But I was wondering if at least the totals under these headings could be given for each of the three services. I am not suggesting that at this stage the minister should try to set up his estimates in a different form. I wonder if he understands what I am asking for.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Probably as we go along
in the consideration of the estimates we shall be able to follow what my hon. friend has in mind. I believe that under the primary headings to which he has referred I can give what amount would stand as carryover from previous commitments. We will follow the practice of distributing to each member of the house an itemized break-down of the total, and if a further break-down of that is needed I will try to provide it.
Progress reported.
It being five minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
